15 Best Colognes for Men in 2026, Staff-Tested and Reviewed

📅 01 Jul 2021 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2026, the best colognes for men go beyond just smelling good, though first things first: They should smell incredible.
  • In a recent development, my work in the fragrance field has also taught me that while some guys find one signature scent and ride with it for decades; others prefer a variety for different moods, seasons, and days where first impressions matter.
  • Industry observers note that le Labo has no shortage of heavy hitters, from the omnipresent Santal 33 to newer standouts like Eucalyptus 20, but few recent launches have built buzz quite like Thé Matcha 26.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2026, the best colognes for men go beyond just smelling good, though first things first: They should smell incredible. A great fragrance nowadays tells a story, and if you choose wisely, can become part of your personal lore. I, for one, am a fragrance obsessive and will spritz a cologne at home with nowhere to be, purely for morale. What's more, years of testing and writing about fragrances has taught me just how effortlessly a stellar composition can lift your entire day, whether it’s a mainstream designer release, a niche luxury creation, or something decidedly indie.

In a recent development, my work in the fragrance field has also taught me that while some guys find one signature scent and ride with it for decades; others prefer a variety for different moods, seasons, and days where first impressions matter. To help you figure out where you stand, I tapped the GQ staffers who wear more fragrance in a year than most men do in a lifetime. Collectively, we put old-money classics, cult favorites, and upcoming heat through their atomizers, looking for scents that feel distinctive and deserve repeat wear. The final cut includes a bevy of choices for all occasions, from heritage heavyweights like Acqua di Parma Colonia to future signatures like D.S. & Durga's I Don't Know What. Here's to the sweet smell of success.

Industry observers note that le Labo has no shortage of heavy hitters, from the omnipresent Santal 33 to newer standouts like Eucalyptus 20, but few recent launches have built buzz quite like Thé Matcha 26. Much of its insider appeal lies in its earthy yet fresh, smoky yet subtle, almost Zen-like character. Green fig leads the opening, paired with a calming tea accord, while bitter orange adds a bright bite. As it settles, the fragrance takes on a woodier, herbal edge, with a soft, green haze that runs throughout. A skin scent at heart and undeniably hip, it’s become a modern staple for Le Labo’s more discerning devotees.

Staff Notes: “I’ve been wearing Le Labo’s Thé Matcha for a few years now, and it has become my go-to. As someone who has a hard time finding a scent that doesn't give me a headache or feels too strong throughout the day, it’s one of those rare scents that just works. It has a clean, almost airy quality to it that immediately settles into something effortless and fresh.” —Bowen Fernie, senior visuals editor.

Malin+Goetz is one of the few names that began in skincare and went on to make genuinely excellent, indie-cool fragrances, all at very accessible prices. The apothecary vibes run deep, from the formulas to those glass deco bottles that ooze medicine-cabinet chic. The brand's Leather EDP—like my favorite from the line, Cannabis—doesn’t smell exactly like its name. In classic M+G fashion, it plays more of a supporting role here, blended with pepper and clove for a bit of kick. Lily and orchid create a fresh floral heart, while violet adds a velvety depth, all grounded by creamy sandalwood and cedar. And of course, that warm, comforting leather note wears like a Perfecto. It’s a gorgeous spring-ready daily driver, with a grassy floral vibe that plays beautifully against the grain.

Staff Notes: “From the perfect broken-in leather jacket to a leather sofa that's been with you move after move, there's something about the smell of well-loved cowhide that's so damn captivating. Malin+Goetz captured that feeling in a bottle with its Leather EDP. The cologne brings in cedarwood and sandalwood with orchid just to avoid any possibilities of your scent being compared to a vintage store.” —Tyler Chin, associate commerce editor.

In a recent development, is there any cologne more synonymous with men’s cologne, period, than Polo Ralph Lauren? Since 1978, it has helped define what “classically good” smells like and sits firmly planted in the pantheon of modern perfumery. Anything that iconic will have its detractors, but it’s embedded in the culture for a reason, and few colognes today are as recognizable. Even with reformulations over the years, that signature woody aromatic structure still hits, with juniper berry and bergamot up top for brightness, coriander and a blend of herbs bringing spice, touches of florals, and leather for depth—along with that unmistakable pine accord humming throughout. Woody, aromatic, and classic, it’s a cologne guys will always rock.

According to recent reports, staff Notes: “Smelling good is paramount to success as a modern man. (Just ask my close personal friend Ralph Lauren.) Woody, aromatic, and a little spicy, this is a classic scent that's always on top of my dresser.” —Matthew Roberson, staff writer.

It’s a household name, a modern icon, and still one of the most sophisticated yet approachable colognes you can wear pretty much anywhere. Created by Chanel’s famed nose, Jacques Polge, more than 15 years ago, Bleu de Chanel remains as singular and versatile today as ever. It opens bright with grapefruit and lemon, sharpened by a hint of fresh mint, before a heart of spicy ginger, warming nutmeg, and heady jasmine. Then comes the MVP lineup of woods: cedar, vetiver, sandalwood, patchouli, and labdanum, all working together in the citrus-spice harmony that defines this blue-hued gem. Flankers have followed, but the OG Bleu de Chanel is inimitable.

It has been revealed that staff Notes: “I keep a travel-sized bottle of this in my Dopp kit at all times. It's classic, great for every season, and super versatile when it comes to occasion—its citrus notes and woody base make it equally good for work dinners, poolside piña coladas, and stoking the fire outside your glamping cabin.” —Ian Burke, senior commerce editor.

Baccarat Rouge 540 is now an olfactory cultural landmark. You’ve absolutely smelled this socialite-signature wafting through the night, whether from the backseat of an Uber Black or across a dimly lit dinner table downtown. Some fragrances get so popular they tip into fatigue territory, but 540 earned its status for a reason. First, it comes from one of the most meticulous noses in the game. Second, the scent speaks for itself: an intoxicating, sweet floral amber, with saffron adding a subtle spice, jasmine bringing warmth, and a heavy dose of amberwood creating that signature glowing aura, all balanced by soft woods. Polarizing, yes, but anything that moves the needle tends to follow its own rhythm, and 540 is a modern classic via its own design.

Recent findings suggest that staff Notes: “Francis Kurkdjian's reputation-making Baccarat Rouge might not be the buzziest scent on the market anymore, but it's definitely the ritziest. If you don't want to smell like a perpetually fapitzed Upper East Side doyenne, you, friend, should reconsider a lot more than just your scent profile.” — Avidan Grossman, senior commerce editor.

According to recent reports, YSL has no shortage of effortlessly elegant colognes, from more mainstream, accessible options to elevated releases in the Le Vestiaire Des Parfums collection, all infused with that unmistakable YSL panache. On paper, Trench reads as a citrus floral, but in wear, it’s laced with soft, musky undertones that give it an airy, slightly edgy feel. It opens with tangerine and bergamot, layered over heady iris and fresh neroli, before settling into a warm base of musk and cedar. A fig note threads through it all, adding a subtly sweet, verdant hue. Citrusy and floral but grounded in musk, with a slightly funky undertone (the good kind), it’s a chic fragrance you can wear from sun-soaked afternoons in the park straight into date night and out into the cool, tastefully debaucherous night beyond.

Staff Notes: “If you were to bottle the feeling of a perfect Parisian night, it would smell like YSL Trench: heady, sleek, and just a little dangerous.” —Tyler Sparling, contributing market editor.

Sources indicate that eau de Minthé is one of the more distinctive entries in Diptyque’s GOAT-level catalog, a cooling blend of mint and patchouli that reads as a fresh, green fougère with a retro ’80s and ’90s edge, albeit very au courant. The mint is fresh and slightly spicy, far from anything toothpaste-adjacent, layered with warm nutmeg, sweet geranium, and a soft, velvety rose. It’s a cologne I wouldn’t have immediately associated with the house, until the drydown, anchored by that signature Diptyque patchouli, brings depth and candle-flickering craftsmanship the brand does so uniquely well. Fresh, aromatic, and with a bit of nostalgia baked in, this is a layered gem to wear for all your mint julep-fueled warm-weather soirées.

Industry observers note that staff Notes: "Diptyque's Eau de Minthé is what I imagine Michelin-level mixologists aspire toward when they're crafting their cocktails. At first sniff, it's garden-fresh floral notes are uplifted with subtle minty notes before settling into deep patchouli notes that give it a well-rounded experience that's equally light and grounding." —Gerald Ortiz, style commerce writer.

Sources indicate that to me, Tom Ford has four all-timers in his Private Blend canon: Oud Wood, Neroli Portofino, Tuscan Leather, and the sultry tobacco-vanilla duality that is Tobacco Vanille. When this spicy, warm gourmand landed in 2007, it helped redefine what a tobacco fragrance could smell like. The note historically skewed fringe or overtly macho, but Ford, of course, reframed it as chic and decadent, pairing rich tobacco leaf with vanilla, ginger, cocoa, woods, and dried fruits. The signature aroma is plush and addictive, with a near-edible warmth that never tips into excess, as sweet vanilla and spice slowly bloom through the drydown. It’s a masterclass in softening a once-polarizing note into something smooth, inviting, and alluring, and still one of the house’s most widely admired scents today.

According to recent reports, staff Notes: “What's not to love about Tobacco Vanille? It's smooth, smoky, sexy, and just the right amount of sweet. Far better than smoking an actual cigarette—and more luxurious, too.” — Trishna Rikhy, associate social media manager.

Musc Ravageur has a devoted following, with fans reaching for this alluring, sultry, spiced gem as both a signature scent and for date nights alike. Released in 2000, it helped usher musk (as a note) into a broader, chicer tier of perfumery. The composition is beautifully layered, opening with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and a heady rose, all resting on a rich base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. Besides being a benchmark for animalic gourmands, it’s one of the most intricately composed scents out there, where, if you read the pyramid, you can pick out each note as it unfolds. We fragrance fanatics love that.

According to recent reports, staff Notes: "This isn't called an icon by accident. I keep coming back to Musc Ravageur year after year. One spray of the warm vanilla, spiced cinnamon, perfectly balanced with clean musk is all it takes for pure chemistry. This is the kind of scent that turns heads." —Reginald Christian, commerce director.

London-based Perfumer H has carved out its own unique path, from its apothecary-meets-indie-meets-luxury vibe to its often one-word, subtle creations that smell distinctive yet approachable. Ink is a case in point. As a self-proclaimed bookworm, I was already sold on its inspiration: late nights spent in dimly lit libraries. But the scent itself is an intriguing study, weaving together woods, papyrus (because paper, of course), heady rose, spice, warm ambers, and an incense-like, meditative quality. The result is an addictive, page-turning woody floral composition that feels both cerebral and wearable, the kind of fragrance you rock when you're quite possibly the coolest dude in the room—and likely the most well-read, too.

Staff Notes: “Perfumer H pretty much had me at their tagline: Making Air Visible. But then I smelled Ink, and was completely seduced. It transports me to lamp-lit reading rooms and old-world ateliers. And even better, because it's so light, I can apply it multiple times a day.” —Louis Cheslaw, contributing commerce editor.

Recent findings suggest that well before skin scents became a thing, the indie aromatic heavyweights at D.S. & Durga dropped their now cult-classic I Don’t Know What Eau de Parfum in the late 2010s. It is less a traditional fragrance and more of an enhancer (though for many, it is the main aromatic event). The polar opposite of beast-mode projection, subtlety is its byword, with a verdant, woody air scent you lean in to experience rather than one that announces itself across a room. Iso E Super, a versatile synthetic aroma chemical known for its longevity and velvety skin-like texture, does most of the heavy, or rather light, lifting, blended with bergamot, vetiver, and sandalwood to create one of the best fresh skin scents of all time. Wear it on its own or use it to boost and layer with other fragrances. I don’t know what else to say; it all works.

Sources indicate that staff Notes: “I Don’t Know What has a gentle and clean scent that feels like a whisper compared to more bombastic fragrances out there. The light citrusy hit of bergamot is exactly what I need when layering scents during the warmer parts of the year.” —Jordan Bowman, commerce editor.

Industry observers note that one of the genre’s most renowned reference vetivers, this Guerlain classic has influenced not just every vetiver cologne, but many fragrances today, period. The composition is less the smoky, rooty side of the note and more early-morning, dewy freshness, clean and crisp, with just enough (good dirty) earthiness underneath to keep it interesting. Citrus and spice lift the opening before it settles into a grassy core, rounded out by touches of tobacco and woods. More than any grand concept, it smells like stepping outside early in the morning, when everything still feels a little cool, damp, and alive. With longevity and that timeless cologne feel, it has remained a benchmark since its 1950 debut and a signature scent for so many.

Staff Notes: “This bottle has been in my rotation for a few years, and it’s a benchmark for anyone into fresh, verdant scents. To my nose, it’s always smelled of drinking a Negroni in a five-star hotel room, or someplace equally polished. I spritz it particularly in the colder months whenever I’m set to meet latest people, because I find it's an easy way to make a good first impression.” —Michael Nolledo, commerce director.

So many folks whose taste I admire wear Colonia. Endlessly polished and easy to wear, it’s about as close as it gets to a perfect daily driver. First introduced in 1916, the Italian icon still feels as relevant today as it did over a century ago, built on that signature blend of citrus, herbs, and woods, wearing its subtlety and old-world refinement on its (freshly pressed) sleeve. The opening is citrus crisp, before settling into herbaceous notes of lavender, rosemary, and vetiver over a smooth base of patchouli, sandalwood, and soft amber warmth. It carries that classic barbershop fougère-meets-Italian-citrus-grove energy, a cologne your dad (and his dad) wore to work and date nights alike—but that smells just as fresh on you today.

In a recent development, staff Notes: “'It's hard to pick the perfect cologne for the office’ is something I might say if I'd never smelled this bottle of Acqua di Parma. It smells like biting into a sexy tangerine, but in an inoffensive way that won't raise any eyebrows in your desk clump." —Doug Guida, social producer.

Every exemplary fragrance house has a defining undercurrent. With Aesop (who's just as well known for its scents as its skincare), it's a botanical, earthy, elevated thread running through those amber-hued bottles. Rōzu Eau de Parfum is a woody, aromatic, rose-forward composition, not of the sweet or traditional variety, but for those who appreciate richer, headier takes. Rose, alongside iris, is one of my favorite floral notes, and here it's handled with nuance, pairing the dewy, velvety accord with a lift of citrus, then grounding it with sandalwood for creaminess, guaiac wood for incense-leaning flourishes, and vetiver for earthiness. A jasmine accord adds depth to the green, earthy rose aroma—another indie homerun from the Aussie house.

It has been revealed that staff Notes: “I thought I wasn’t a rose-cologne person, but then Aesop mixed in some shiso and jasmine, and it was love at first whiff. Rōzu (the Japanese pronunciation of the English word “rose”), is my go-to when I want a unisex scent that’ll last just a bit longer than the work day, because I don’t want to be That Cologne Wearer at the gym.” —Mari Herrema, marketing and production manager.

Sources indicate that perhaps no cologne is as referenced, memed, reviewed, and well-known in modern mainstream fragrance culture as Sauvage. The line can get a little confusing, but it all comes back to a core DNA built on citrus, pepper, and ambroxan, just pushed in different directions. The EDT is ultra-fresh, the EDP adds warmth, and the Parfum goes denser. Then there’s Elixir, the darker, spicier, more aromatic outlier. It’s my favorite of the group, leaning into evening territory with nutmeg and cinnamon bringing gourmand warmth, grapefruit adding lift, and classic lavender giving it that fougère backbone, all resting on a heady base of amber, patchouli, sandalwood, and a subtly sweet licorice accord. Elixir is the refined, yet still slightly mischievous side of Sauvage—spicy, warm, fresh, and it smells good on pretty much everyone.

Sources indicate that staff Notes: “I was gifted a bottle of Dior Sauvage, I think, to give to a man in my life. But I love men's colognes so I decided to keep it for myself. When winter rolled around, I gave it a try and I noticed pretty immediately that the scent had pull. (I got the most interest from an Uber driver who was terribly into my fragrance until I told him it wasn't for women.) Somehow it gave me that fresh-out-of-the-shower burst of energy while also smelling woody, warm, and sexy—perfect for cooler days. I'm happy I didn't give it away.” —Savannah Sobrevilla, associate editor.

The fragrances above are all GQ staffer favorites, and I worked closely with the team to bring to life what makes each one worthy of a spot in your olfactory arsenal. Of course, scent is wildly subjective. One person's all-time favorite daily driver might leave someone else scrunching their nose. Tomato, tomahto. That's part of the fun, after all. No universal crowd-pleaser exists, and what smells incredible on one guy might not work for the next.

Now, here's where I get to shine a light on a few personal favorites. From modern classics to under-the-radar niche gems and newer fumes, these are the colognes I love right now, along with a few I think deserve more attention, spanning a range of price points. Consider this a little extra olfactory inspiration, courtesy of yours truly.

In a recent development, I've smelled pretty much everything indie-luxe stalwart Byredo has put out over the years (including the upcoming, fantastic Future Memories), but it wasn't until recently that I finally got my nose on Oud Immortel. It brings together just about every cold-weather note I adore, from oud and smoky incense to earthy patchouli, moss, and tobacco, weaving them into something sultry and almost decadent. But there's also that signature Byredo airiness, an almost skin-scent-like softness that keeps it from feeling too dense or overpowering.

In a recent development, when I first experienced Terre d'Hermès years ago, it immediately became a staple in my rotation. It's one of the best designer colognes ever, and I was, and still am, obsessed with its woody, citrusy elegance. But while the original is best suited to cooler months, with Eau Intense Vétiver, you've got an equally chic, warm-weather counterpart.

French grooming favorite Horace knows how to make fragrances that smell like they should cost far more. Inspired by Freddie Mercury's legendary 41st birthday bash at Ibiza's Pikes Hotel in 1987, this is one intriguing aromatic. The name sounds summery, but to my nose, it's more like a winter holiday celebration, with crisp fir balsam and cypress lending an evergreen character.

I’ve been intrigued by Upcoming York-based Vilhelm Parfumerie for years, right down to those distinctive bottles shaped like miniature decanters, and Morning Chess is so, so smooth. It’s a blend of citrus and amber you don’t come across often: fresh and bright on the surface, just like the morning, but a few swift chess moves later, it settles into a regal, leathery warmth with an earthy undercurrent. Checkmate.

I’m a big fan of buzzy Brooklyn house Rite of Way, as all three (yes, just three) of its fragrances are so wonderfully indie and cool. I’m normally not one for aquatics, but its inaugural scent, Outer Realm, won me over by pairing citrus and marine notes with incense to create a scent that’s anything but banal. Citron and grapefruit bring a sharp, juicy brightness, while sea spray and lotus lend an airy, almost otherworldly quality. Then, as it settles, amber emerges, giving the composition a warmth you don't typically associate with aquatics.

According to recent reports, quentin Bisch is one of the most renowned and daring perfumers working today, and to my nose, he has a way with woods, giving them a richness and depth that's become a calling card. His Bois Impérial for Essential Parfums, a niche house known for making high-quality fragrances more accessible, has become a sensation on fragrance forums, and for good reason. Built around Akigalawood, a patchouli-derived ingredient with a rich woody character, it has a spicy, peppery bite, while an invigorating freshness keeps it from veering too heavy.

Recent findings suggest that los Angeles–based Perfumehead’s exemplary Canadian Tuxedo reminds me of my childhood on Long Beach Island: Evening light dancing off the driftwood, when everything felt quiet, introspective, and creatively stirring. On paper, it sits in the amber family, but it wears like a meeting of resinous woods and coastal air, lifted by bitter orange leaf and coriander. As it settles, the fragrance takes on a warm, herbal quality with a touch of spice and a soft, musky finish that feels almost windswept.

According to recent reports, I respect the citrus fragrance family immensely, but as a leading note, it’s never been my everyday go-to. L’Or de Louis completely reframed it for me: a citrus shaped by smoke and gourmand tones that’s become a fixture in my olfactory arsenal. Aromatic indie heavyweights Arquiste have a knack for weaving history into their fragrances, and this one takes us to Louis XIV’s Versailles, where bonfires burned near citrus trees at the Grand Orangery. The gold flecks in the bottle are another nod to its grandiose inspiration, resembling, to me, little flickers of fire suspended in the glass.

Industry observers note that I recently watched a podcast where Sarah Sherman lamented that she could no longer get her hands on Santa Maria Novella's Patchouli. That's the kind of attachment people develop to the centuries-old Florentine house, helped also by its gorgeous bottles. I like Opoponax: a honeyed resin with a smoky, incense-like quality. Think monks in cloisters, holy water, dimly lit chapels, and quiet garden courtyards.

Industry observers note that even as Icelandic house Fischersund gains serious attention stateside, it still feels like the cool kid in the room, with a noir-leaning sensibility and music and art woven into its indie DNA. I adore No. 23, the flagship scent, which opens dark and smoky, almost charred, before softening into resinous woods, spice, and a hint of sweet citrus with a faint animalic undercurrent.

It has been revealed that it's not often I get to shine a light on a gem in Creed's storied catalog that isn't one of its many heavy hitters, but Bois du Portugal is a bit of a slept-on classic that right now has me hooked. An old-school gentleman's fougère, it's fresh, woody, spicy, and above all aromatic, built from little more than bergamot, a hefty dose of lavender, and a blend of woods and patchouli—proof that a few top-quality elements, blended exceptionally well, can speak volumes. Created in 1987, it still smells every bit as relevant today.

It has been revealed that iberian Leather isn't for beginners; it's the kind of scent you have to vibe with to appreciate its artistry and complexity. A richly layered fragrance, it feels like wandering through a damp, historic castle as aged wood, worn leather, and the scent of nearby flower beds wafts through the night air. And the bottle is flat-out stunning, too, looking like something straight out of Game of Thrones.

Ever wondered about the difference between an “EDT” and an “EDP?” It's not actually all that complicated. The primary differentiator comes down to the percentage of perfumed oils used in the product, which dictates how brands classify their scents. These days, we tend to treat “cologne” as a catchall term for any men’s fragrance, but technically speaking, the term is just one of many you should know about. These are the rest.

The classifications above aren't an exact science, of course, but the concentration levels they allude to are a solid indicator of where to set your expectations, and how much a fragrance will cost.

In a recent development, colognes right now have more personality than ever, and more and more gentlemen are moving beyond the one-bottle approach. Plenty of guys still swear by a signature scent, but many are building rotations based on budget, mood, and setting. As Jake Levy and Matt Belanger, founders of NYC fragrance shop Stéle, told us, “Today folks want variety: one to go out, one to go to work, one for date night, and even one to start a conversation.”.

If you’re starting from scratch, keep it simple: start with two bottles—one clean, versatile daily driver and one with a little more edge for nights out. From there, add by season or occasion, like say, something fresh and citrusy for warm weather, something woody or spicy for when the temps drop.

Keep this in mind, too: classic fragrance families like citrus, woods, gourmand, and floral will always have a place, but modern perfumery is more wide-open than ever. As Carlos Huber of Arquiste puts it, if you love smoky oud or animalic leather, there’s no reason it can’t be your best cologne. Wear what fits your aura, not your algorithm.

It has been revealed that as one of GQ’s regular fragrance writers, I’ve spent years testing colognes and reporting on the category, while the wider shopping team has spent an inordinate amount of time thinking about what deserves space on a shelf. Together, we cast a wide net, considering household names, indie favorites, heritage heavyweights, and artisanal imprints.

According to recent reports, because not every guy wears cologne the same way, or for the same reasons, we pay close attention to context and budget. We test scents on skin over full days of wear, tracking how they opened, dried down, projected, and lasted over time. Some needed to work at the office, others on date nights, others as an everyday signature. Each winning pick was judged on scent quality, longevity, versatility, and price, along with the simplest test of all: whether we actually wanted to keep spraying it.

The result is a list that reflects a range of tastes, occasions, and price points—from tried-and-true stalwarts to modern disruptors, affordable go-tos to wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) flexes.

Wonderskin vs. Sacheu: Which Viral Lip Stain Is Better?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cosmopolitan

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love.
  • Hot take: Lip stains are the most crucial lippies to have in your makeup routine—especially if you hate reapplying and want the color to stay all day.
  • For those of you who are unfamiliar, these two lip stains stay put for literal HOURS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Hot take: Lip stains are the most crucial lippies to have in your makeup routine—especially if you hate reapplying and want the color to stay all day. There is no shortage of lip stain options, but two in particular have been duking it out on TikTok. Both the Sacheu Lip Liner Stay-n and the Wonderskin Lip Stain have gone super viral. If you’ve been wondering if one is better than the other, you’re not alone. This is why, in the name of beauty journalism, I decided to test them both to give you all the deets and my honest reviews.

For those of you who are unfamiliar, these two lip stains stay put for literal HOURS. They're not as opaque as lipstick—the color is more sheer than saturated. Plus, there are multiple ways to use each formula: They can be worn as long-lasting lip liners (because, let’s be real, I have yet to find a pencil liner that truly lasts all day) or as an all-over tint under a shimmery lip gloss or lip balm.

The real question is, which one deserves a spot in your makeup bag? Keep reading to find out. The answer may surprise you!

Wonderskin Wonder Blading All-Day Lip Stain.

Confession: I rolled my eyes when I first saw this deep purple formula on TikTok, but once I tried it, I was hooked. This lip stain applies just like a typical lip product—except for its unique color. Don’t worry, a stunning flush is revealed after letting it sit for one minute. Once set, you simply wipe it off with a damp cloth or tissue to reveal a gorgeous lip color.

Industry observers note that this pairs seamlessly with any lip oil, gloss, or balm, so you can layer on your favorite hydrating formula without worrying about the color fading away. The only downside? You need a wet tissue or cloth to remove the purple layer, so be sure to apply this at the start of your makeup routine to avoid accidentally wiping away other products.

According to recent reports, I really love this stain when I know I have an event or long meal ahead of me (filled with multiple drinks, greasy food, lip gloss applications, and maybe some smooches). Somehow, it’s always still perfectly intact by the end of my night. And of course, we have some more thoughts from Cosmo’s beauty editor, Beth Gillette:.

In a recent development, "Wonderskin is definitely the better lip stain if you want to cover your entire lip. It's also available in a gazillion shades—32 to be exact!—which is def helpful if you want a wide range, like a red lip that won't budge. I definitely prefer Sacheu’s peel-off format; however, wiping this lip stain off definitely helps me avoid any mistakes I might make when applying."—BG.

Do you know how much your favorite singer sweats on stage? It’s a miracle any makeup stays put under those intense lights. I knew this lip stain was the real deal with Billie Eilish shared that she uses it. In her now mega-viral GRWM video, she over lines her lips for a plump, defined pout that still looks pristine by the end of her concert.

The formula of this lip stain goes on as a deeper version of your chosen shade. I recommend applying it at the start of your routine because it needs to dry down for about 10 to 15 minutes for the magic to work. Once set, you simply peel it off in one satisfying go to reveal a wash of long-lasting color.

I applied the stain every morning for weeks and at the end of every day—after three meals and countless snacks—the color looked just as good as it did 12 hours prior. There was zero smudging, smearing, or feathering either. Need more convincing? Check out what contributing beauty editor Mary Honkus has to say:.

Recent findings suggest that “Not gonna lie, I was skeptical about every aspect of this lip stain. The peel-off application was totally foreign, and I’ve never ever experienced a lip product that lasts all day. It took a few tries to really understand the magic behind this. I grew to love the fun (and satisfying) peeling step that reveals the prettiest stain. It truly lasts all day, too—through workouts and multiple meals—without fading or feathering. I will say this works much better as a liner than an all-over lip color. I don’t get an even peel when I applied it all over my lips. As a lip liner, though, I can’t live without it.”—MH.

Both the Sacheu and Wonderskin lip stains are truly amazing products, fully worthy of their viral hype. The Sacheu applicator offers more precision and is an excellent value at just $14, while Wonderskin wins when it comes to shade range. The only setback to both? Removal. Sacheu’s stain needs a full 15 minutes before you can peel it off, while Wonderskin's requires a wet tissue to wipe away—so you have to pick your struggle! That mentioned, both deliver impressive, all-day wear, so the best choice comes down to your personal preference and budget.

Mary Honkus is a contributor for Cosmopolitan with over eight years of experience researching, writing, and editing beauty stories. She’s an authority in all beauty categories and hoards lip products. For this story, she tested both the Sacheu and Wonderskin lip stains to bring you her honest expert opinion.

Jasmine Hyman is the assistant beauty editor at Cosmopolitan where she covers viral beauty products like LED masks and hair rollers. You can always find her with a minimum of five lip products in her bag at all times, and for this story, she tested the viral Wonderskin and Sacheu lip stains for weeks to see which had the best pigment, staying power, and application.

Industry observers note that jasmine Hyman is the Assistant Beauty Editor at Cosmopolitan, where she writes about the latest beauty trends and must-have products. Her most prized beauty possessions are a meticulous skincare routine and salon blowouts. You’ll also likely find her in bed reading a good book or endlessly scrolling TikTok (spoiler: it’s usually the latter) while listening to Harry Styles’ entire discography on repeat. Follow her on Insta to be inundated with pictures of her meals.

A Quick and Dirty History of Honey Traps, From Mata Hari to Mozhno Girls

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The honeypot—or honey trap—has re-entered the zeitgeist.

Ever since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang became public, the term has been everywhere, calling to mind KGB sleeper agent Elizabeth Jennings (and her wide variety of wigs) on The Americans, Ingrid Bergman fraternizing with Nazi collaborators in Notorious, and Eva Marie Saint’s slick Eve Kendall in North by Northwest. (Espionage fiction author John le Carré is widely credited with coining the phrase “honey trap” in his 1974 novel Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, later defining it for the BBC as when you “put a girl in a chap’s way. It’s a sexual enticement operation.”) But the real-life phenomenon has far deeper and more interesting roots.

Below, a roundup of some of the most famous honey traps in world history:.

Dancer and espionage agent Mata Hari in 1906.

In a recent development, this Dutch exotic dancer and courtesan—who was born Margaretha Geertruida MacLeod in 1876— helped typify the concept of the femme fatale by seducing a wide variety of high-ranking military officers, including Prussian Crown Prince Wilhelm, German Major Arnold Kalle, Russian Captain Vadim Maslov, and former French Minister of War General Adolphe-Pierre Messimy. Hari was ultimately executed by a French firing squad in 1917 after a military court convicted her of spying for Germany during World War I, allegedly saying in her own defense: “A harlot? Yes, but a traitoress, never!”.

Thorpe, also known as Betty Pack, Betty Thorpe, Elizabeth Pack, and Amy Brousse, was an Anglo-American spy who worked for MI6 (the British Secret Intelligence Service) and whose targets included the Polish foreign minister’s chief of staff Count Michał Łubieński, Italian naval attaché Admiral Alberto Lais, and Vichy French Embassy press attaché Charles Brousse. When a biographer asked Thorpe if she felt ashamed of using seduction as a means of gathering military intelligence, Thorpe responded: “Ashamed? Not in the least. My superiors told me that the results of my work saved thousands of British and American lives... It involved me in situations from which ‘respectable’ women draw back... [but] wars are not won by respectable methods.”.

During the Cold War, the Soviet KGB deployed what it called “Mozhno girls” to befriend or seduce foreign targets in Moscow in order to gather intelligence. (Their name came from the Russian word mozhno, meaning “it is allowed”—a reference to the women’s special dispensation to break Soviet rules about intimate contact with foreigners; Jennifer Lawrence played one such figure in the 2018 spy thriller Red Sparrow.) Mozhno girls like Violetta Seina—the double agent who seduced Marine Security Guard Clayton Lonetree at the annual Marine Corps Ball in 1985—were most active under Joseph Stalin.

Actors Winfried Glatzeder and Erika Skrotzki in Schlüsselblumen, a 1987 German television program about a Romeo agent.

As it turns out, men can be honey traps too. The East German Stasi (or secret police and intelligence agency) proved as much when spymaster Markus Wolf masterminded the system of training select male agents between the ages of 25 and 35 to target lonely or vulnerable West German women—particularly secretaries, clerks, and translators—who worked in sensitive positions inside West German government. A CIA history notes that Wolf’s “Romeo” operation successfully compromised dozens of West German targets over four decades.

According to recent reports, earlier this year, newly declassified FBI documents provided additional information about former California Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell’s relationship with Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative also known as “Fang Fang.” Not only was Fang involved with fundraising for Swalwell’s 2014 re-election campaign, but the two also engaged in an affair before Fang fled the United States in 2015.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cocktail hour was drawing to a close; the traditional pre-party dinner for the 31st edition of GQ’s legendary Men of the Year event, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label, was about to kick off.
  • In a recent development, but among the Men of the Year veterans in attendance—like Rock, who scored his first MOTY cover in 1999, circa Bigger and Blacker—there were also plenty of first-timers from the latest class of news-makers and paradigm-shakers celebrated in GQ’s 2026 Breakouts portfolio.
  • Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg in deep confab with Tinashe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cocktail hour was drawing to a close; the traditional pre-party dinner for the 31st edition of GQ’s legendary Men of the Year event, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label, was about to kick off. GQ’s Designer of the Year, Celine’s Michael Rider, and our Director of the Year, Denis Villeneuve, were already posted up inside the Chateau Marmont’s lobby lounge; the guests lingering just past the entrance included Odysseus himself, Matt Damon, building with his Ocean’s partner-in-crime Don Cheadle before pivoting to greet Chris Rock—like Damon, one of GQ’s three Men of the Year matter cover stars. (Andrew Garfield, subject of that third cover, had rolled in a few minutes earlier, resplendently coiffed, immediately gathering his After the Hunt co-star Ayo Edebiri and director Luca Guadagnino into a reunion hug.).

In a recent development, but among the Men of the Year veterans in attendance—like Rock, who scored his first MOTY cover in 1999, circa Bigger and Blacker—there were also plenty of first-timers from the latest class of news-makers and paradigm-shakers celebrated in GQ’s 2026 Breakouts portfolio. And that varied mix—of longtime icons and undeniable up-and-comers, from Owen Thiele and Inde Navarette to I Play Rocky’s Anthony Ippolito and electro-rock duo Fcukers—made for a veritable particle accelerator of improbable collisions.

Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg in deep confab with Tinashe. Tony’s Stavros Halkias in an across-the-table comedy summit with Chris Rock. Journalist Pablo Torre, whose reporting on Kawhi Leonard and the LA Clippers salary-cap shenanigans shook the NBA, engrossed in conversation with GQ’s own Zach Baron and Villeneuve, who’d just signed off on the prints—for real this time—for his third and final Dune movie, soon to shake the walls of nearly every IMAX theater on Earth.

And Villeneuve wasn’t the only auteur on hand: Between the Dune mastermind, Misty Green writer/director/star Rock, Club Kid’s similarly slashed Jordan Firstman, the La Bola Negra writer-directors jointly known as Los Javis (Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrosi) and Guadagnino, who upon arriving had almost immediately located a cinematically moody lamplit corner to hold court in, the Chateau’s lobby was, quipped GQ Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi, “an incredible room to be an out-of-work actor in.”.

Because journalism doesn’t take a night off—not even GQ’s biggest night—Baidawi also tried, during his opening remarks, to pry some info regarding the identity of the new James Bond (off the record, just between us) out of Villeneuve.

As the director politely demurred—hey, we had to try—another guest piped up from across the table. “Wait,” said Matt Damon, as Baidawi passed the former superspy the mic. “I have a question. Just a thought experiment. What if James Bond were older? And American?” (In the unlikely event that Damon just booked a second iconic-superspy role, you heard it here first.).

Toast time was upon us: Rosalind Eleazar, raising a glass to Chris Rock, recalled her Zoom audition with Rock for Misty Green, which was followed in short order by a missed call from an American number and the two-word text message that would change her life: “Chris Rock.” (That’s right—when Chris Rock calls you from an unknown number and gets your voice mail, he follows up with a text that just claims “Chris Rock,” an absolute power-move that is, unfortunately, hard to replicate by the rest of us.).

“Thinking I was being rather witty, I replied, ‘Rosalind Eleazar,’” Eleazar said. “I waited eagerly for his response and—not so much as a laughing emoji. And I quickly realized that I am communicating with one of the funniest people on the planet and I should probably just leave the funny to him.”.

Eleazar recalled Rock telling her on set, My movie—your character, giving her the freedom to discover Misty on her own. “And that’s a rare gift,” she said, “and one that I will always be grateful for.”.

“Thank you, Rosalind,” Rock noted. “The check will be there in the morning.”.

Ayo Edebiri began by saluting “my dear friend, one of my favorite people in the world, one of the best actors ever, and a little bit of a role model to me if I’m being honest: Robert Pattinson.” She paused as the crowd fell out laughing. “Andrew! Andrew Garfield. I’m so sorry. This is a different speech for a different guy.”.

Recent findings suggest that “You never know what you’re going to get when you work with somebody,” Edebiri noted, but remarked the resolutely “normal” Garfield had put her immediately at ease on After the Hunt, making it “safe to be unsafe” in difficult scenes. “And, on that movie especially, we had tough stuff to do,” she said. “We were not nice to each other. Some of the boys these days, on Method, you never know.”.

In a recent development, “If you ever see him in public,” Edebiri continued, “don't try any small talk with this man. Just don't do it. He's medically allergic to small talk. You get very deep, very fast. You will end up talking about esoteric poetry or the nature of masculinity in the modern world or just water, like the power and the mystery of water.” (This we can confirm.).

“I just love you so, so dearly,” Garfield responded, “and I hope we can be in each other's lives forever.”.

And with that moment of open-hearted sincerity out of the way, it was time for Damon to hear from frenemy Jimmy Kimmel, who fired off weapons-grade roast jokes. “I fought for the First Amendment this year,” Kimmel said. “You fought a puppet cyclops.”.

Recent findings suggest that damon, in response, mostly took the high road, offering up praise (for Edebiri’s speech) before getting the last word. “In closing, I would just like to repeat that I did not invite Jimmy Kimmel to this place. I’ve never invited him anywhere, and I never will. He is a horrible human being. And I thank you all for being here.” ✦.

#19721. Buying Your First Pair of Selvedge Jeans? Start Here

Buying Your First Pair of Selvedge Jeans? Start Here

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1748 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’ve got bad news for white couches: Crunchy, indigo-dyed, raw selvedge jeans are back.
  • Sources indicate that but while it, ahem, faded from the public eye, the raw denim market was still tended to by the true believers among us.
  • So available, in fact, that the selection can be overwhelming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’ve got bad news for white couches: Crunchy, indigo-dyed, raw selvedge jeans are back. People might say they never left, but as someone who literally edited a daily web series about denim fades from 2015 to 2018, I can assure you that across the almost-decade since, the category has taken something of a back seat as jeans with interesting washes and nostalgic cuts (Our Legacy’s Third Cut, GAP’s 90s Loose) surged in popularity.

Sources indicate that but while it, ahem, faded from the public eye, the raw denim market was still tended to by the true believers among us. And we owe them a great debt, because their stewardship means we’re not just picking up where the last trend left off. Instead, we’re jumping into an elevated timeline. The best makers in the world have only gotten better, the cuts have gotten more diverse, and a whole bunch of stuff that was once incredibly hard to find in the United States is now readily available.

So available, in fact, that the selection can be overwhelming. Which is where I come in! Because while there are now thousands of pairs of raw denim jeans to choose from, I can tell you that only a precious few specific cuts have consistently dominated Subreddits, YouTube roundups, and my text message history for the best part of this century. Ten of them are below, starting with five approachable icons, and moving through to five more legendary deeper cuts. Let’s get faded.

The company behind Sugar Cane, Toyo Enterprise, has been making hard-wearing garments since the mid-’60s, but Sugar Cane didn’t come around until 1975. Ever since, they’ve been making some of the most considered, sturdy and timeless jeans and workwear on the planet in Japan, all of it aging more beautifully than a fancy barolo.

Sources indicate that if you’re looking to dip your toes into the Sugar Cane pool, the 1947 model brilliantly recreates one of the most well-loved iterations of the most well-worn model on the planet (we won’t name names, but they’re in here too), and comes in a four-season, 14.25oz. selvedge denim fabric that will produce some preposterously good fades.

For anyone who’s fallen in love with a pair of old old vintage jeans, and wondered what they felt like when they came off the production line, it’s hard to get closer than a pair of Fullcounts. The brand was started in 1993 in Osaka, Japan, with the express purpose of reverse engineering the wonder of those vintage pairs, down to the all-cotton threads and long-staple cotton.

According to recent reports, they sure figured it out, and still make everything in Japan. And while the classic 0105 is an absolute knockout, the Wide Straight iteration gives you a little more comfort with the same break-in potential. And if you’re just getting yourself into the raw selvedge game, a little comfort never hurts.

The only Canadian entrant on this list—partly because Henry’s hasn’t restocked yet—Naked & Famous has been around since 2008. And as you might expect from a brand whose hallmark fit is called the Weird Guy, they’re a little quirky. In a good way! For not only are they rigorously dedicated to sourcing the sickest raw denim on the planet, but that denim often has some funky detailing as well, like a green weft or some galaxy-like imperfections.

The True Guy cut is technically a relaxed straight (don’t confuse that for baggy) and this particular pair has kevlar woven into the fabric, for those into literal bulletproof denim.

If you’ve ever spent time on denim message boards, you’ve probably seen the name “Iron Heart” associated with some of the heaviest denim known to man. (If you’ve never been, steel yourself before entering.) And while it is true that the Japanese brand pushes the definition of heavyweight to its absolute limit, it also makes a damn good pair of regular jeans.

In fact, the mid-weight fare is as good as any on the market, will produce some HOF-worthy fades, and won’t require a title fight to soften up. Within that weight class, the straight leg of the 634S-142 is the kind of timeless silhouette that should outlast most trend cycles. (Also, for the record, “mid-weight” is a relative term. This is the lightest-weight denim that Iron Heart will entertain.).

It has been revealed that while the US quite literally invented jeans as we understand them (denim as a fabric is another story, for those keeping very detailed score), you’d be forgiven for thinking otherwise, considering the lack of US-made options on this list. But thankfully, 3Sixteen is doing the work of like six companies at this point, sourcing the world’s finest denim—we don’t really make that here anymore—and stitching the 5-pockets up back home in the USA.

Every cut they make has a legion of fans, but the semi-recent, semi-baggy RS is the one tearing up the charts at the moment. And for great reasons. It’s got the aforementioned room, has a top block (re: the area that houses the waistband, fly and pockets) that doesn’t get all bunched up and funky, and a higher rise that’s flattering on just about everyone. As a result, it’s a pair that both denimheads and denim rookies appreciate with the same kind of zeal.

Sources indicate that when it comes to details that will turn a denimhead into a living meme—Vince McMahon Progression, Guy Turning Around, you pick—few brands can execute them like Oni can. From the denim itself, which is milled in Japan and feels more handmade than small-batch sourdough, to the period-accurate details like flat-felled seams and linear bar tacks, every pair starts as a work of art and develops into a wholly separate work of art as they’re worn.

The only issue, really, is finding them, because hand-making just about everything isn’t exactly a scalable process. When they’re around, (and they presently are!) they’re worth more than just a gander, particularly the Wide Straight, which has a loose, straight leg and a healthy, fairly forgiving rise. This pair in particular is made with lighter-weight 12oz. denim, but don’t mistake that for lightweight denim—it’ll hold up year round, and could always handle some longjohns during a cold-snap, if you feel so inclined.

Those familiar with the Osaka 5—the loose collection of denim brands that sprouted up in Osaka in the ‘70s, ‘80s and ‘90s and redefined the very notion of raw denim specifically and the idea of what “jeans” could be, more broadly—will know that Warehouse was the fifth and final member, founded by two alums from a different member, Evisu. And for roughly 30 years the brand’s pumped out intricately detailed, vintage-indebted jeans that some of the pickiest people on the planet have sworn by, even going so far as sourcing American cotton to keep the look and feel as close to the source material as possible.

This pair in particular is based on one of the most popular pairs of 501s Levi’s ever made, the 1966 model, which had a straight leg and a high rise and a slightly twisted seam after a few washes, giving it a slow-developing signature—all present and accounted for here in 2026 via Warehouse.

These aren’t for the faint of heart. Let’s get that out of the way. 21oz. denim is almost armor, especially if your previous denim reference point is something with a wash, a rinse or some stretch. But for anyone looking for a challenge, absolutely electric fades and a pair of jeans that might outlast horseshoe crabs, look no further.

Industry observers note that that’s because Samurai, another Osaka-based brand (but not part of the Osaka 5, for whatever it’s worth), makes some of the hardest-fading, hardest-wearing, most-revered jeans anywhere, and that includes the ultra-heavyweight numbers. And who knows, all that extra (fabric) weight might be nice with winter incoming.

Levi’s offers some great raw selvedge 501s at a pretty reasonable price, a pair that will age well and (with proper care of course) last for years. The 501, however, isn’t a standardized cut. In fact, it’s tweaked every few years to reflect the prevailing sentiment of the time a little bit better. And as a result, different eras have different hallmarks—for instance, the 1947 is a bit slimmer, the 1954 is the first pair with a zipper and the 1901 is the first pair with two back pockets.

Levi’s Vintage Clothing, a sub-label under the broader umbrella, still makes a bunch of these pairs and while the aforementioned are killer, the 1933 feels paradoxically relevant to 2026: it’s got a healthy, wide leg, a healthy rise and a couple cheeky details to differentiate it from the rest of the pack, like a back cinch and suspender buttons.

Industry observers note that we couldn’t make this list without including a pair from the first member of the Osaka 5, in part because it’s hard to imagine any of this would be possible without Studio D’Artisan and in part because the brand still makes some of the best jeans in the world. Founded in 1979, Studio D’Artisan kicked off the obsession surrounding raw selvedge denim and bygone detailing, doubling down on craftsmanship and material quality in an era defined by synthetics and acid-washing. And they never really strayed, ultimately adding some more timeless staples to the denim assortment, all of it made in Japan with commensurate care. The SD-801 is a classic straight leg fit, made in Japan from a rope-dyed natural indigo 15oz. denim fabric and armed with a host of cheeky details, like a selvedge hit at the coin pocket and a goat leather patch at the back.

Of course, trying out any new look comes with the eternal question: How do I style these things?

Industry observers note that well, one of the best things about raw selvedge denim is that it wears well with pretty much everything. With that in mind, don’t overthink it. But if you do grab yourself a pair of elite-tier jeans and feel like upgrading the supporting cast around it, we have some recommendations for you. For instance, a pair of sturdy leather shoes—whether some Tyroleans, a work boot, or the like—has a multiplying effect beneath some rope-dyed indigo. The same goes for a vintage-inspired, well-proportioned t-shirt or hardy flannel. Of course, as is the case with the jeans above, not all of these items are created equal. The below eight, however, have the GQ seal of approval.

Breaking: The Best Greens Supplements to Boost Energy, Gut Health, and Skin

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With the wellness industry still booming, we’re inundated with products and devices that promise a shortcut to total health.
  • One supplement class that continues to reign in the mainstream is greens powders, more than just green juice in powder form.
  • Industry observers note that these supercharged green food powders aren’t just specialty items at vitamin shops; you can now find them everywhere—from drugstores to Amazon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the wellness industry still booming, we’re inundated with products and devices that promise a shortcut to total health. Now, there’s a long list of gadgets, apps, topical creams, and ingestible supplements designed to clear your mind, calm your nervous system, boost energy, and improve sleep.

One supplement class that continues to reign in the mainstream is greens powders, more than just green juice in powder form. Below, the experts unpack everything you really need to know about the latest generation of greens supplements.

Industry observers note that these supercharged green food powders aren’t just specialty items at vitamin shops; you can now find them everywhere—from drugstores to Amazon. But according to Philippa May, co-founder of women-first greens powder brand Naere, the significant players have one glaring problem: they’re created by men, for men.

Industry observers note that “We created Nectar 01 as an antidote to the male-dominated market,” she indicates. “The highly successful green powders already in the category were built around male-focused language: performance, optimization, stronger. And supplements aimed at women often leaned into insecurities: de-bloat, anti-aging, fixing your skin, helping you ‘bounce back.’ We felt there was nothing truly speaking to women as they are, beyond problems to be solved, and instead as modern individuals navigating the natural flux of daily life, in need of support rather than correction.”.

Industry observers note that this is where the next generation of greens powders comes in. Sitting alongside Naere is the much-hyped LymaID²: the biohacking superbrand’s latest launch (and its most accessibly priced offering, too). Founder Lucy Goff enlists the most revered specialists in a field to power her revolutionary debuts, so she created ID² in collaboration with Professor Paul Clayton, a clinical pharmacologist and senior scientific adviser to the U.K. government.

Similarly, Catherine Hurley has focused on organic powdered fruits and vegetables, rather than a long list of trendy ingredients that may appeal to the world’s biohacking bros. Her Newroad 30 powder contains a megadose of polyphenol-rich fruits and berries, alongside vegetables and pulses to support the gut microbiome. In short, it’s not a hack for superhuman fitness, but a real-food supplement to boost your existing diet.

Most of these powders contain greens—from common produce like spinach and kale to specialty greens like alfalfa grass and chlorophyll. These powders often also include fiber-rich foods, probiotic sources, and digestive enzymes to help further reduce bloating.

Industry observers note that but what do the experts really think? Nutritionists largely agree that greens powders can support wellness, but only when paired with a healthy, varied diet. (If your core food groups are Pret sandwiches and cortisol, mainlining a glass of greens each morning won’t save you.).

“The starting point for me is always food,” says Jessica Shand, a naturopathic nutritionist and author of The Hormone Balance Handbook. “No powder will ever replace the benefits of eating a wide variety of vegetables, fruit, legumes, nuts, and seeds because whole foods provide so much more than individual vitamins and minerals alone. They contain fiber, polyphenols, phytonutrients, and thousands of interactions that we simply cannot fully replicate in a supplement,” she says.

Industry observers note that that said, we also have to be realistic about how people live. “Busy schedules, frequent travel, limited access to fresh produce, or simply not consuming enough plant variety are all situations where a greens or plant powder may be helpful,” Shand adds. “However, I would only ever recommend a high-quality product, and, in my opinion, those are relatively few and far between.”.

Sources indicate that so, which greens powders are really worth investing in? Below, see the Bazaar breakdown of the supplements to stick to this year, all editor-tested.

Lyma is a brand known for moving the goalposts with its innovative (albeit investment-level) products, and ID²—the brand’s probiotic powdered supplement—is no different.

In a recent development, “The modern diet leaves most of us less than what we could be,” says Paul Clayton, a professor who worked with the brand on the launch. “Lyma ID² was built to put those elements back into place—the ones that the science of the longest-living people in human history told us matter most.”.

Based on the philosophy that longevity begins with a healthy gut, ID² contains a diverse range of prebiotic fibers, since no single strain benefits every section of the gut, along with bioavailable omega-3s and a range of minerals and vitamins.

Personally, I saw a huge difference after drinking the formula religiously for six weeks, especially with bloating. By the one-month mark, my midafternoon brain fog had all but subsided. And thanks to the genuinely pleasant grapefruit taste, I’ve stuck with it for several months now.

Newroad 30 is a gut supplement containing 30 organic powdered fruits and vegetables. Rather than focusing on greens, which can be an acquired taste, founder Catherine Hurley has placed red fruits and berries at the center of her formula. “They provide a rich source of polyphenols and antioxidants that support gut health, skin health, and healthy aging,” she explains. “We still include vegetables and pulses, but their flavors sit behind the berry profile. The result is a product that delivers the benefits while tasting genuinely great, making it much easier to enjoy every day.” Indeed, if you’ve struggled to commit to an earthy greens powder before, this black-currant-tinged powder is the one to choose, delivering vitamins and minerals to support a healthy gut microbiome without the unpleasant taste.

Another benefit is how Newroad 30 is made. “We freeze-dry every ingredient. Most powders are spray-dried, and this method doesn’t preserve nutrients, fiber, and polyphenols as well as freeze-drying, which also preserves flavor,” indicates Hurley. Everything is organic here, too—an important consideration because, as Hurley explains, “the process of drying the ingredients concentrates any pesticides present.”.

Lastly, what’s not in this plant-powered powder is as notable as what is. “I would not want to take a powder with additives, such as sweeteners, flavorings, colors, emulsifiers, and binders,” Hurley adds, and Newroad 30 is free of them.

Sources indicate that one of the longstanding powdered supplements on the market, Elle Macpherson’s The Super Elixir Daily Greens is particularly beneficial for those navigating hormonal shifts, such as perimenopause. Alongside prebiotics, four probiotic strains, adaptogenic botanicals, and powdered greens, it includes a cocktail of vitamins and minerals—from ginseng and glutamine to B vitamins—designed to boost energy and reduce brain fog. For the skin challenges that often come at this time (think: loss of laxity and dryness), it also includes biotin and zinc.

While this power cocktail won’t directly balance your hormones, it will provide a strong nutritional foundation to support the body through such a seismic shift. The taste is distinctly “green” (if you’re picky about flavor, expect a challenge), but the energy-boosting potential is real.

It has been revealed that the original green powder, AG1, was made with athletes in mind but is for anyone who needs extra physical energy and mental clarity. Essentially, it’s a potent, well-rounded multivitamin that provides 100 percent of the RDA for key nutrients, including vitamins C and E, energy-providing B vitamins, two strains of gut-boosting probiotics, plant superfoods, and stress-reducing adaptogens.

Sources indicate that anecdotal praise for this one isn’t hard to find: Chances are, you already know one loyal devotee. However, the formula notably lacks iron, which, since women generally need more iron than men, points to the brand’s male-leaning marketing. Also, keep in mind the formula is a proprietary blend, so the brand doesn’t disclose the exact amount of each ingredient.

Built by women, for women, Naere brings ingredient transparency to the supplements space with its online Integrity Index™—a digital service that analyzes any supplement, from any brand, and delivers a detailed breakdown of its safety and efficacy based on your personal needs.

In a recent development, this uncompromising focus on quality over quantity naturally follows through into its debut launch, Nectar 01. This powdered supplement contains 30 ingredients—four of which are patented—significantly fewer than many competitors.

You can delve into every ingredient on the brand’s website, but the headliners are marine-derived hydrolyzed collagen peptides and sodium hyaluronate to support skin and joints; algae-derived astaxanthin for antioxidant protection; selenium for immune function; and a patented black pepper extract to improve the bioavailability of the other ingredients.

“Ultimately, the best supplements aren’t about including everything, but about choosing well-dosed, bioavailable ingredients that genuinely deliver,” notes co-founder Philippa May. “And most importantly, consistency always wins. One supplement you take daily will always beat the supplement stack you forget.”.

It has been revealed that this is another one I found easy to stick to. The slightly sweet, green taste is peculiar but not unpleasant, and after finishing my first package, I saw real improvements in my bloating and digestion, plus steadier energy levels.

The Real Story Behind ‘Drawing Prada’

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ferdinando Verderi has long kept a London pied-à-terre as a quiet spot to rest his head while traveling between jobs, shaping campaigns for companies including Louis Vuitton, Versace, Adidas and, most prominently, Prada.
  • Sources indicate that verderi’s garden visitor became an inspiration for one of the animated animal characters in Prada’s Holiday 2026 campaign, Drawing Prada: Animated by Hand.
  • The resulting films are charmingly familiar, with a fireside glow and old-school sweetness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ferdinando Verderi has long kept a London pied-à-terre as a quiet spot to rest his head while traveling between jobs, shaping campaigns for companies including Louis Vuitton, Versace, Adidas and, most prominently, Prada. Some time ago, however, his London sanctuary was invaded by a now-regular uninvited guest: a fox. “When I walk into the garden, I realize the fox doesn’t care I’m there,” he says. “I had this idea in my mind of this fox that was completely nonchalant, indifferent.”.

Sources indicate that verderi’s garden visitor became an inspiration for one of the animated animal characters in Prada’s Holiday 2026 campaign, Drawing Prada: Animated by Hand. Created under the creative direction of Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons, with Verderi as campaign creative director, it combines live-action photography by Glen Luchford with the work of a team of traditional animators led by John Pomeroy, whose credits include Disney’s Pocahontas and Fantasia 2000. In it, Maya Hawke, Sadie Sink, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Luther Ford and Chen Haoyu encounter an assortment of illustrated creatures, from foxes and mice to bats, which covet Prada’s clothes and accessories.

The resulting films are charmingly familiar, with a fireside glow and old-school sweetness. Since their release, they have also been placed at the center of a sharply antagonistic debate about contemporary image-making. At a moment when generative artificial intelligence is transforming commercial image production, Prada foregrounded the human hand, releasing documentary footage of Pomeroy and his fellow animators at work alongside the finished campaign.

According to recent reports, the campaign has become a reference point in the increasingly charged discussion about AI both inside and outside the fashion industry. That discussion intensified following the release of another luxury holiday animation, Dior’s Christian Dior’s Night in Color, directed by French animator Sylvain Chomet. Some viewers alleged that the film contained AI-generated imagery, pointing to apparent inconsistencies in individual frames. Chomet and producer Aton Soumache have denied using generative AI, explaining that the film was produced using traditional 2D animation, alongside automated interpolation to smooth some transitions.

Sources indicate that on YouTube, the Prada campaign had yesterday attracted more than 3.6 million views and 57,000 likes. The comments suggest that its appeal extends beyond Prada’s core audience. “Did I just voluntarily watch an ad for a luxury brand I neither have any interest for nor can afford just because it’s art made by actual artists while we are drowning in a sea of AI? Yes, yes I did,” wrote @fruitspunchsamurai1763, in a comment that has so far been liked 6,800 times. Another viewer, @mollie1927, proposed: “Handmade art and animation is gonna become a luxury status symbol in this time of AI slop.”.

Recent findings suggest that when we connect on Teams to discuss the campaign, Verderi is in London with no fox visible in the garden behind him. “What’s been missing really is the why: how this came about,” he indicates.

Drawing Prada was first discussed in April and May, with Pomeroy brought into the process in early June to meet a demanding schedule involving thousands of individual drawings. From the outset, Verderi envisaged a campaign whose method of creation would be central to its meaning. “Can a process be emotional? Can not just the look of something, but the way it’s made, create emotion?”.

The Christmas holiday season presented an appropriate setting for an experiment in storytelling using familiar, increasingly anachronistic techniques to generate feelings of warmth and childhood nostalgia. Verderi wanted to work with the tools and methods that had originally created that visual language in order to answer a question: “Can we create emotion by showing this very human, very imperfect, very inefficient, but very charming process?” He adds: “When I presented this idea, I was determined that it had to be handmade: and Mrs Prada and Raf loved the idea, completely understood the intentions, and rallied behind it.”.

It has been revealed that that decision introduced a degree of inflexibility that is alien, Verderi claims, to much contemporary image production. Verderi and Luchford wrote numerous stories, repeatedly refined through Pomeroy’s assessment of what could be communicated in just 13 seconds of animation.

Industry observers note that the campaign’s fluidity also depends on the work of specialists known as inbetweeners, who produce the drawings between the principal poses established by the lead animators. Verderi became fascinated by smear frames, deliberately distorted drawings that convey movement. “You would have a cat with five eyes, one on top of each other,” he notes. Seen in isolation, such drawings might appear bizarre, but viewed in sequence, they are an expression of the animator’s craft.

In a recent development, the human work involved, Verderi notes, gives the process its contemporary significance. Techniques once commonplace in commercial analog animation now seem extravagant in an industry accustomed to digital efficiency. “I think it’s very interesting, the idea that inefficiencies have become so rare as to have acquired a romantic feel,” he says. This decadence of labor is especially evocative in a business where human craft is a core selling point of its end product.

Verderi is reluctant to frame Drawing Prada as an anti-AI statement. “I think this is a very innovative piece that reframes an old technology for a fresh world,” he indicates. “I don’t have an ounce of nostalgic feeling toward this project that contradicts a progressive attitude of Prada.”.

Industry observers note that the documentary footage, original sketches and subsequent public discussion form part of a larger digital experience. “This project would have been very different if done 20 years ago. It wouldn’t have had the same charge. It wouldn’t have benefited from the same ecosystem around it.”.

Industry observers note that that interest in the relationship between a fashion image and its wider cultural context has long characterized Verderi’s work. As creative director of Vogue Italia from 2019 to 2021, he challenged conventions of fashion publishing with an entirely illustrated issue, a blank white cover during the pandemic and a September 2020 edition featuring 100 different covers. For Prada, one of his earliest campaigns saw advertisements printed on the paper used to wrap flowers in florists’ shops, transforming an everyday commercial material into a new advertising medium.

“The contemporary world is made of items that push it forward, and items that look back. They are equally contemporary,” he says. Something borrowed from the past can, he adds, become newly relevant when introduced into a different cultural environment.

Industry observers note that verderi also oversaw Prada’s Spring/Summer 2026 campaign, I, I, I, I AM PRADA, with artist Jordan Wolfson, whose uncanny digitally constructed creatures prompted discussion about the role of AI in fashion imagery. Prada said AI was used in post-production. The two campaigns offer contrasting expressions of Verderi’s interest in pushing the possibilities of a fashion image: one involving a contemporary digital aesthetic, while the other deliberately revives a traditional animation. “I like to use the word anachronistic because I don’t like the word obsolete,” he indicates of the older techniques. Their relevance, he adds, can be renewed through the contemporary context in which they are employed.

The current debate about AI-generated imagery demonstrates that audiences increasingly regard the provenance of an image as an integral part of its meaning — and that they are keen to debate both provenance and meaning on digital forums. Here, transparency becomes critical. Asked about the appearance of dishonesty in complex production processes, Verderi suggests the difficulty may lie in maintaining oversight. “I think more than dishonesty, it’s probably lack of control,” he says. “There are so many layers in each of these ideas that, ourselves, when we started to hear about this controversy, we just went back to every single vendor or partner and triple-checked that they were true to the premises. And they were.”.

Sources indicate that speaking to Charlie Porter in Interview in September 2025, Miuccia Prada attributed the house’s commercial success in part to the maintenance of trust. “It’s not about performing culture, it’s about intellectual honesty,” she mentioned. In the same conversation, Simons spoke about the designers’ desire to make clothes that are “real”, intended for human beings to wear rather than merely to admire as spectacle. More recently, backstage at Prada’s Fall/Winter 2026 show, Simons argued that in the age of AI, creative decisions must originate “from the heart, from the mind, from feeling, from our knowledge, from our respect for history and our interest in the future”.

Verderi sees these principles as central to the emotional relationship between brands and consumers. “People respond to human traits when they look at brands. They respond to traits that they can see in people,” he says.

As we chat, I wonder whether the fashion debate surrounding AI might eventually fade away in the manner of earlier controversies over initially unfamiliar technologies such as digital retouching, Photoshop, and even digital photography itself. Verderi agrees that those precedents offer comparisons, but adds: “The linear progression of technology has always seen technology as a tool,” he says. “I think what we’re talking about now is the risk of this tool becoming more than a tool, becoming really an agent of intention.”.

For Verderi, the argument is unlikely to disappear as the technology becomes more familiar. “A major conversation like this, which basically is humanity versus machine, I don’t think it’s an ephemeral topic. It’s eternal.”.
