  • In a recent development, I caught Damon at the entrance to the party looking to continue our conversation from his cover story, but our reunion was cut short when Inde Navarette pulled up to say hi and exchange contacts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there’s no party quite like a GQ party. Who else could bring together Andrew Garfield, Robby Hoffman, Future, and Angel Reese under one roof? But that’s exactly what we did on Thursday night at Los Angeles’s famed Chateau Marmont for our 31st Men of the Year party, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label, with special thanks to the 1 Hotel West Hollywood.

Following a dinner honoring our trio of cover stars—Matt Damon, Chris Rock, and Garfield—the real fun began when all three of them, along with nearly every other celebrity in town, descended on the Chateau’s garden to mix it up to the sounds of DJ Yung Tada (plus a late-night set from GQ Breakouts electro-pop duo Fcukers).

In a recent development, I caught Damon at the entrance to the party looking to continue our conversation from his cover story, but our reunion was cut short when Inde Navarette pulled up to say hi and exchange contacts. If the 25-year-old Obsession newcomer was starstruck by the 56-year-old Hollywood hero, the feeling seemed mutual.

Future and Travis Scott rolled up nearly at the same time; Travis, who performed the end-credits track for The Odyssey, told me he was ready to hit the Oscars campaign trail.

In a recent development, in every corner was a cluster of stars from different Hollywood galaxies. Abbott Elementary’s Tyler James Williams and Chris Perfetti made the rounds together, looking nothing like the harried teachers they play on TV. GQ Breakout Owen Thiele and his longtime friend Cazzie David (who gave Owen his first acting gig on her web series years ago) ignored our red carpet instructions to bless us with photogenic poses they’d pre-planned long in advance. When I asked broadcaster Taylor Rooks for an on-the-fly NBA Cup prediction, she gushed about the Celtics and the Lakers. And there was something fun about seeing Anderson .Paak and Diplo chop it up, too.

The friendly embrace shared by Austin Abrams and Skyler Gisondo, noted Good Dudes, is the unscripted team-up the internet goes nuts for. The Resident Evil and Primetime actors later shared that they’d just been on the phone together while getting ready for the party, neither realizing they’d be seeing each other shortly. When I brought up James Gunn and his recent departure from DC Studios, Gisondo called it a “bummer”—he just wrapped the “Jimmy Olsen vs. Gorilla Grodd” series, he said, and hopes that it’ll still come out (and that Gunn continues to write and direct even if he’s not in executive mode anymore).

In other unlikely but endearing encounters: Ayo Edebiri and Thiele excitedly nabbed IShowSpeed for a photo, and Lamorne Morris stopped Anthony Ippolito to give him props for I Play Rocky, counseling him to take it all in. Ippolito told me he’s headed off to Europe soon to continue promoting the film; a certified foodie, he was hunting for Paris recs (I had to put him on to HolyBelly, for the pancakes). I also caught GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, whose eyes lit up when I mentioned his woefully underrated Jake Gyllenhaal thriller Enemy.

According to recent reports, midway through the night I spotted Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro, who were considering an Irish exit. Garfield’s forthcoming Artificial (out December 25) is the movie on everybody’s lips, but he told me he’s looking forward to spending the holidays in New York and taking a brief break before what will probably be a busy campaign season for the Man of the Year.

Industry observers note that no one captured the evening as succinctly as Robby Hoffman, who described her upcoming TV show as “Curb [Your Enthusiasm] for poor people.” When the conversation turned back to GQ, Hoffman rued the decline of magazine paper quality. But this latest glitch got her seal of approval: appropriately glossy, well-considered, and elite to the touch. Though she might have just been describing the party’s guest list.

Sources indicate that but even if you didn’t make the cut, you can see how GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party looked from the inside. ✦.

#19708. Tech Report: How Tecovas Is Taking Western Mainstream

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1770 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: How Tecovas Is Taking Western Mainstream

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for CEO David Lafitte, Tecovas can outlast cowboycore.
  • “There is this cultural zeitgeist going on, and I think we’re kind of in the bullseye of it, so that’s a good thing,” Lafitte notes.
  • According to recent reports, now, Tecovas has surpassed $400 million in trailing 12-month revenue, marking almost 40% year-over-year growth — one of the strongest stretches in the company’s history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for CEO David Lafitte, Tecovas can outlast cowboycore. In fact, he believes Westernwear isn’t a trend at all.

“There is this cultural zeitgeist going on, and I think we’re kind of in the bullseye of it, so that’s a good thing,” Lafitte notes. Cowboycore peaked in 2024 on the heels of Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter album, Pharrell Williams’s Western-inspired Fall/Winter 2024 Louis Vuitton collection and the series finale of Yellowstone. Tecovas, which specializes in cowboy boots and was founded in 2015 by Paul Hedrick in Austin, benefited from the boom.

According to recent reports, now, Tecovas has surpassed $400 million in trailing 12-month revenue, marking almost 40% year-over-year growth — one of the strongest stretches in the company’s history. When Lafitte joined the company in 2022, revenue was around $150 million. The brand now has 69 stores across the US, from Austin to cities like Boston, New York, Miami, and LA.

It has been revealed that “We want to make sure that we stay authentically Western, and we can’t worry about the trends. If we try to move around too much, we’re going to lose our DNA and our anchor. There are a lot of people in the middle of the country for whom this is their lifestyle. It’s not a fad or a trend.”.

Sources indicate that eleven years in, Tecovas has cowboy boots down pat. Now, the brand is looking at how to grow its Westernwear offering without falling into the traps of fleeting trends or diluting its original USP: well-made, authentic Western footwear at an accessible price point. Though the brand intends to remain footwear-led, as Lafitte puts it, it’s also investing more in men’s shirting, womenswear and accessories. Belts and wallets have been doing especially well, he notes. Still, the brand’s boots — most of which sit in the $300-400 range — remain the entry point to the brand. “People are still coming in for the boot,” he states.

11 years in, Tecovas is taking the western aesthetic mainstream.

According to recent reports, tecovas’s ethos is best expressed in-store, Lafitte argues. Physical retail accounts for 60% of the brand’s revenue. “It’s a product that I think is key for people to see, touch and smell as soon as you walk in our doors,” he claims. It’s also where shoppers then encounter the brand’s wider range. “We’ve got a lot of traffic in our stores, so when we come up with compelling products, we’re able to showcase that and don’t need to necessarily spend a lot of marketing dollars on shirts or other things — because we have that audience coming into our doors,” Lafitte says. He points to the Monterrey slip-on loafer: not traditionally Western, not necessarily what you think of when you think of Tecovas, but the style still does $7 million in annual revenue. And many buyers likely already have a pair of Tecovas boots at home.

Sources indicate that tecovas sits at an interesting intersection in the US fashion ecosystem. As European luxury brands are scrambling to increase their presence in the country’s southern and southwestern states, Tecovas is going in the opposite direction. States like Texas, Colorado, and Tennessee are Tecovas’s strongholds. Now, the brand is pushing into fast-growing regions including the Southeast, Midwest, and West Coast.

In a recent development, with four funding rounds totaling $130 million, Tecovas is well positioned for growth. Here’s how the brand is making the cowboy aesthetic mainstream — without falling into the trappings of the often derided “concrete cowboy”.

It has been revealed that lafitte is conscious that, even as the brand grows, authenticity is key to sustained growth and success. That the Western aesthetic has become more mainstream has cleared the way. “People are seeing that to have a pair of cowboy boots in their closet doesn’t mean that ‘I’m just going to a costume party’. You can wear it with other things that may not be Western,” the CEO says. “We need to make sure we stay in our lane, and we need to make it cool. That’s part of what our job is as a steward of this genre: to make sure it’s cool and authentic.”.

It has been revealed that this logic has informed Tecovas’s approach to retail. The brand held off on branching out into wholesale until 2024, almost 10 years into its founding. But it was a priority for Lafitte. “If you’re not in a multi-brand format and your product’s not there, you’re going to be out of sight, out of mind,” he states.

Industry observers note that but the approach was careful, and started with independent Western stores. “They cater to a very authentic Western consumer,” Lafitte indicates. “Our goal is to create an ecosystem. We almost want to drive traffic to their stores, so we’ll do joint billboards and do some marketing tactics that drive consumers to their stores to look for Tecovas products.” The goal isn’t necessarily to then bring them to Tecovas directly, he says, though this would be the dream. “I don’t think that’s going to happen,” he concedes. “These consumers have been shopping with their favorite Western retailer for many, many years. So that’s not the point.”.

The brand keep close ties with independent western retailers.

The point, instead, is to stay in step with the brand’s beginnings while expanding beyond specialty Western retailers. The brand entered 20 additional Nordstrom locations in the spring, and is now in a total of 35 doors. It’s intentionally measured, the CEO says — he doesn’t want Tecovas to be everywhere, lest the brand risk overdistribution. “We want to go with a little bit of a scarcity model, so you can’t find us on every corner of every city and get overexposed.” The goal of these select fashion accounts, he adds, is to reach a customer they may not otherwise; and to establish a presence in regions where opening a store might not make sense due to limited traffic.

“The traditional Western retailers give us that authenticity, the authentic consumers that are buying the brand,” Lafitte indicates. “And places like Nordstrom that are a little bit more fashion, that may be expanding the tent a little bit more, but they too want us to make sure we’re authentic, the real deal — and not some concrete cowboy, or whatever you want to call it.”.

To meet these consumers where they are, Tecovas is tapping into the modern brand-collab playbook, with other brands, sports teams, and musical artists. To Lafitte, anybody can be a Tecovas customer, because anyone can integrate a cowboy boot into their wider wardrobe. He’s banking on a high proportion of music and F1 fans being fans of his brand, too. But, Lafitte insists, its approach is reserved. “I’d rather have very good partners that sort of align with our craftsmanship and ethos and then do them very well and not try and rush them.”.

The latest launch is a tie-up with Los Angeles-based Anine Bing that includes shoes, belts and cowboy hats. A single weekend delivered the sales and unit movement originally forecast for the month, according to the brand, with several styles selling out. Still, the goal for these collabs isn’t to drive revenue so much as awareness, the CEO notes. “It’s more a brand heat moment and awareness gain,” he says. “We’re getting exposed to a consumer base that might not otherwise know Tecovas.”.

In a recent development, the brand takes a similar approach to the sports it taps into; recent partnerships include NASCAR and PGA golf. Neither are the most obvious picks for a Westernwear brand, but there’s a method to the madness. “We’ll test with some upper funnel work, and when we see a pretty good return on that ad spend, then we know that’s an area that we’ve got consumers in that demographic,” Lafitte states. NASCAR driver Ryan Blaney was already a fan, which made him a good fit, he adds. “Consumers are very smart, so we make sure we’re partnering with people who would be wearing the brand regardless of whether we’re giving them product or writing them a check.”.

The Anine Bing collab outperformed expectations.

Tecovas is choosey about which brands it collaborates with, and when.

Music works in the same vein. Tecovas has partnered with country music stars including Ella Langley (it sponsored her “Choosin’ Texas” music video) and Ryan Bingham (it sponsored his, as well as Langley’s, tours earlier this year). But country ties aren’t the only marker of a good partnership. Lafitte points to Noah Kahan, who he met when the singer came into the South Congress store. “He loves Tecovas and brought his team in there,” he claims. “When you see him at his Dallas concert, I think probably 80% of that crowd was wearing boots,” he adds. This combo made the partnership a no-brainer.

“The interesting thing is that Western is resonating across a lot of these different areas, whether it’s music, food, race car driving — F1,” he indicates. “The drivers love coming to Austin, and that’s been a fun thing to partner with a lot of their drivers.”.

Tecovas’s sports and music activations thus far may have centered on the US, but the brand has international ambitions. For Fall 2026, Tecovas sold its first international stock to German multibrand retailer Zalando. When we speak, Lafitte has just returned from Paris, where he met with a handful of retailers including Le Bon Marché. He first met their team when they visited the brand’s Soho, Newly introduced York store. The strategy is to lean on local European distributors, rather than rush to open a European HQ, the CEO adds. “We’ll choose distribution partners and do it in an asset-light manner. We’ll start with wholesale, and then, over time, open a couple of doors with a partner over there.”.

Down the line, the goal is to go public, Lafitte indicates, though he doesn’t have a set timeline for this. (It won’t be in the near-term, he adds, since everything is AI-focused at the minute.) “We want to work toward that knowing that we need to lay the groundwork to be an independent company,” he says. “I don’t want to skimp on, say, ‘we don’t need a distribution center because it’s likely we'll get bought by X, Y, or Z’. We’ve got to make sure that, operationally, we’re laying the groundwork to keep up with the demand.”.

“The brand’s got broad shoulders,” he says. “I think we can be the steward of the West, but we can also, I think, launch a lot of Western-adjacent type products.”.

Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (403 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken.
  • More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.
  • Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Sources indicate that heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Recent findings suggest that add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

  • Recent findings suggest that nike and Adidas lead the way with collaborations from massive designers and some up-and-comers alike, including one release that makes a strong argument for being the best sneaker of the year.
  • Who remarked anything about Samba fatigue?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as we inch towards the end of the year, there’s always a massive holiday rush in the sneaker industry (in addition to, well, everywhere else). Annual seasonal drops like the reliable Black Friday and Holiday XI launches from Jordan Brand, plus every major label trying to end the year on the highest note possible, make November and December some of the most exciting times to be a sneakerhead. To be fair, 2026 certainly still has some gas in the tank—plenty of us are already looking ahead to the return of the “Space Jam” Air Jordan 11 next month. Still, this week stands out even in an already crowded release calendar—in fact, I’m inclined to say it’s the biggest and best week of sneaker releases this year has had to offer so far.

Recent findings suggest that nike and Adidas lead the way with collaborations from massive designers and some up-and-comers alike, including one release that makes a strong argument for being the best sneaker of the year. Reebok’s gradual revitalization takes a massive step in a fun, innovative upcoming direction. And over at Converse, one of the most reliable celebrity designers in the footwear world is dropping some of his best work yet. Start drafting an apology letter to your credit card for everything you’re about to do with it—these are just a few highlights from the biggest, boldest week of sneakers in 2026 yet.

Who remarked anything about Samba fatigue? Turns out all it takes to make one of the most gen-pop shoes of the last decade feel brand fresh is a take like the one offered this week by Adidas Consortium collaborator Invincible, a Taiwanese brand that’s quickly establishing itself as a can’t-miss partner for the Three Stripes. Alongside a stellar line of apparel the brand has savvily outmaneuvered any semblance of cultural exhaustion with one of Adidas’s signature silhouettes by keeping it simple: They’ve outfitted the silhouette in a premium black unstructured leather and, bafflingly, a dress shoe sole rather than the Samba’s traditional gum rubber. With perforated Stripes and detailing that mimics those found on dressy leather brogues, it’s an instant contender for sneaker of the year…even if it just barely qualifies as one. This one goes on sale on November13, but with a catch—it’s an Asia exclusive. Pray to the resale market gods.

According to recent reports, nike has been struggling to find their next major-name collaborator, but in the meantime, some old favorites are still holding strong. One of those names is Union, the Los Angeles-based boutique founded by streetwear giant Chris Gibbs. This week, the brand is offering a buzzy iteration on the classic Nike Dunk that comes in a luxe brown suede and a heel-less mule silhouette. Like the Invincible Samba, the MO here is that all it takes to make an old shoe feel newly introduced again is a left-of-center take. These are dropping via SNKRS and Union on November 13, for $130 a pop.

Through Reebok’s ups and downs over the last decade, there has been one shining constant: Allen Iverson, the greatest athlete they’ve ever had on their roster. AI’s shoes are always in style, so if the brand simply brought back the original Question Mid silhouette for the shoe’s 30th anniversary, it’d be noteworthy enough. This year, though, they’ve taken the shoe to a newly introduced and fairly innovative space, refitting it with modern performance enhancements, making it court-worthy for the first time in decades. Sure, you can still wear them with oversized tees and baggy shorts. But for the first time in ages, the Question could also make it back onto an NBA court (or at least the pavement at your local park). It’s priced at $170 and is available now via Reebok and select retailers.

Sources indicate that ever since he first inked a deal with Converse in 2017, Tyler, the Creator has been one of the best celebrity collaborators in the sneaker biz. This has only become more true since the launch of the 1908 Project last year. The endeavor has seen the pair diving deep into Converse’s archive to revive everything from classic nautical boating shoes, to a jogging silhouette that hadn’t seen the light of day in decades. Ahead of Tyler’s annual Camp Flog Gnaw festival last year, he and Converse debuted their best work at the time: the Bronco Boot, a canvas and rubber-toed banger of a sneaker-boot. This year, they’re running it back on a low-top Bronco Boot silhouette—once again ahead of the festival, where we’ll likely see Tyler wearing them. Think of it as the Doc Martens 1461 to the original Bronco Boot’s Doc Martens 1460. Coming your way in four earthy colorways, these are on sale now via Converse.

Speaking of Converse and boots: One of the biggest sneaker stories of the year has been Rick Owens’s return to Adidas after a fruitful stint over at Converse. The designer’s much-anticipated return collection introduced this week, with these stunners at the center of the capsule. Debuting on the runway at Paris Fashion Week this past summer, Owens’s Springblade boots are a showstopper of a return. The shoe’s upper is made from a loose textile that fits up over the ankle and a leather toe cap, but the real heat comes in the return of the Springblade sole Owens and Adidas first debuted over ten years ago. They retail for a crazy $850, and can be purchased via the Adidas Confirmed app. Rick’s gonna Rick!

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

According to recent reports, place 1–1¼ lb. boneless Fresh York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

According to recent reports, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

In a recent development, meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.).

Recent findings suggest that uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

In a recent development, combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

Industry News: From Nike to Selfridges: GTA VI Is Coming for Fashion

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1623 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a chilly morning last week outside Selfridges, gamers formed a line under the pink glow of a huge neon sign decorating the exterior: I <3 VC.
  • Industry observers note that vice City is the fictional, Miami-inspired setting for Grand Theft Auto VI, but its impact in the real world is already astronomical.
  • The London department store is capitalizing on that energy with a GTA VI-themed pop-up, featuring a 60-piece merchandise collection that includes £8 Vice City keychains, £50 hot pink logo tees, and a patch-covered varsity jacket for £2,500.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a chilly morning last week outside Selfridges, gamers formed a line under the pink glow of a huge neon sign decorating the exterior: I <3 VC.

Industry observers note that vice City is the fictional, Miami-inspired setting for Grand Theft Auto VI, but its impact in the real world is already astronomical. Billed as the most anticipated entertainment launch in history, the video game finally goes on sale this Thursday, with pre-order sales already shooting past $1 billion, breaking records for PlayStation and Xbox.

The London department store is capitalizing on that energy with a GTA VI-themed pop-up, featuring a 60-piece merchandise collection that includes £8 Vice City keychains, £50 hot pink logo tees, and a patch-covered varsity jacket for £2,500. Sounds pricey, until you spot the sky-blue supercar, modeled after the in-game Grotti Cheetah, parked on the ground floor: yours for £1 million.

According to recent reports, charles Hambro, co-founder and CEO of Geeiq, a data platform that has worked with brands including Gucci and L’Oréal to build strategies in the gaming world, states that now that video games are downloadable, the physical aspect of the activation takes on a new charm. “It’s a fantastic moment for GTA fans to come together and meet in real life and celebrate the title and the game and the launch,” he says. “Now that everything’s digital, it’s wise for Rockstar [the publisher behind the game] to hold onto that physicality.”.

Recent findings suggest that the partnership is a win for the department store, too. “The response has been extraordinary,” says Rebecca Warburton, Selfridges’s marketing and experiences director, who worked with GTA’s publisher Rockstar Games on the launch. “[There’s] a real sense of excitement for the collaboration. It’s been fantastic to see the GTA community join us to experience it for themselves, bringing a fresh audience and energy to our stores.”.

The pop-up is part of a raft of major retail activations that Rockstar is rolling out for the launch, which include a Nike collaboration with Travis Scott on a GTA VI-themed Air Force sneaker, and a pair of matte black sunglasses with reflective blue lenses by Oakley that are part of a merchandise box sold on Rockstar’s website.

In a recent development, emy Cies, Women in Games ambassador and projects administrator at the Fashion Innovation Agency at London College of Fashion, notes that these kinds of physical products help widen the appeal of both the game and the brands or platforms that get involved. “Because GTA is so huge, it has that pull between consumers that are absolutely going to play the game and then consumers who are in it for the cultural wave,” she says.

It has been revealed that for Adam Cheung, style writer at British GQ, the overlap between gamers and fashion fans may mean a more engaged consumer base, but the product itself still needs to stand up. “A collaboration gives them a way to bring those interests together, but they’ll still have opinions about the product,” he indicates. “The association with GTA might get their attention, but the design and price will help determine whether they actually buy it.”.

Industry observers note that when images from the game were released in the run-up to the launch, netizens swiftly pointed out similarities between real-life brands and the clothes characters were wearing in-game. The list includes a white Birkin-like handbag, Rolex and Audemars Piguet watches, monogrammed Gucci-esque sweatpants, Chrome Hearts jeans, and a hoodie that recalls Versace’s black-and-gold Barocco print.

Sources indicate that the GTA franchise has long parodied fashion. Jokey-sounding brands like Güffy (a nod to Stüssy), Le Chien (perfume that bears a resemblance to Chanel No. 5) and Ferruccio Tucci (its logo similar to Massimo Dutti) have appeared in previous titles in the series. “GTA has always excelled at satire and social commentary, and fashion and style is part of that,” indicates Jian DeLeon, men’s fashion director at Nordstrom. “It does a good job of fleshing out a world and giving players who care about style the option to express themselves accordingly.”.

According to recent reports, julie Zerbo, a Latest York-based lawyer and founder of The Fashion Law, says these spoofs highlight an interesting tension at the heart of luxury marketing. “Luxury brands work to maintain exclusivity, but their cultural influence depends, in part, on widespread recognition,” she says. “The more recognizable a brand becomes, the easier it is for others to reference, imitate, or parody. That visibility can be commercially valuable, even when the brand has no control over how it is being represented.”.

In a recent development, this lack of control is not necessarily a negative thing. “Appearing in a game this big could introduce them to people who haven’t paid much attention before, especially with labels that are more familiar within fashion circles,” states Cheung.

Recent findings suggest that zerbo notes that inclusion in the game, even as a parody, is a measure of a brand’s real-world relevance. “[These brands] communicate certain qualities to consumers, which makes them obvious subjects for a game that draws heavily on popular culture and consumerism,” she says. “In some cases, being recognizable enough to be referenced without permission is itself evidence of the value of the brand.” Neither Rockstar nor the parodied brands replied to a request for comment.

With the in-game fashion representing its own socioeconomic system that ranges from thrift stores to luxury boutiques, players graduate from tank tops and cargo pants to Italian suiting and loafers as they expand their influence in the city’s criminal underworld. GTA VI also introduces the franchise’s first female protagonist in the form of Lucia Caminos, meaning we can expect to see plenty of options for in-game womenswear. “It opens up the game a lot more [in terms of fashion], so I think that will be massive,” states Cies.

Recent findings suggest that though there is precedent for in-game brand collaborations (GTA Online featured clothes by the Polish brand MISBHV back in 2021), product placement is rare in Rockstar’s games. But in the same way that GTA borrows the language of fashion to create in-game parodies, brands can also co-opt the aesthetic of GTA. Gucci, for instance, released a campaign in February that featured AI imagery of a couple sitting on a car bonnet in front of a neon pink Gucci sign. The visuals were unmistakably Vice City, and a neat way for the brand to tap into the zeitgeist.

Social teaser campaign ahead of the Gucci Primavera campaign in February 2026.

Hambro also references recent images posted to BMW’s Instagram that feature illustrations that draw on the pink, palm tree-heavy aesthetic of the game. “That’s a brand that has sort of managed to circumnavigate; they’re involved without getting involved,” he indicates. “The core point is that there’s going to be a lot of people playing this game, and a lot of those people are going to be firmly within the target market of a lot of these companies. The question is, how are you going to engage with them?”.

It has been revealed that dazed saw the game’s potential early. For its Fall 2026 concern, the magazine collaborated with Rockstar to put GTA VI’s dual protagonists on the cover. “The anticipation surrounding GTA VI was unlike anything we’d seen in gaming or entertainment,” notes Danil Boparai, Dazed’s content strategy director. “We knew how hungry the game’s fanbase was for newly introduced information. We wanted to create something that would reward that anticipation while introducing the game to audiences who might not traditionally engage with gaming media.” When the story went live, it became the most-read article on the Dazed website in a decade.

Recent findings suggest that as gaming has become more mainstream, perceptions of its audience have shifted. “The cultural relevance of gaming is something that no longer needs explaining to brands,” claims Hambro. “The preconception of who the gamer was in 2007 probably would’ve been an acne-ridden young boy in their mother’s basement. And now it’s Travis Scott.”.

Though GTA VI will be limited to single-player at release, it is expected that it will eventually expand into a multiplayer online experience. GTA Online, the multiplayer component of GTA V, reportedly earns over $1 million in daily revenue with 10 million weekly active customers. “For Gen Z and Gen Alpha, their version of socializing is going into a game together and chatting and playing and hanging out,” notes Hambro. “They just might happen to be doing it in Gucci Town in Roblox, or on GTA Online.”.

Recent findings suggest that for many players, gaming is also becoming less about playing as a ready-made character and more about creating one that reflects their own taste and identity. According to a recent report by Dentsu, 65–70% of Gen Z and millennials who play games say they can express themselves more easily in games than in real life. With games like GTA VI offering increasingly sophisticated options for customization, clothing becomes a way for players to construct and communicate who they are. “It’s [about] creating a world where identity isn’t just something you select, but something you actively shape through your choices,” says Boparai.

Sources indicate that will the aesthetics we see in the game translate IRL? DeLeon is skeptical. “I don’t really think there will be a huge effect on how people dress in the real world, but I’m sure there will be parallels with the kind of brands and clothes that are glorified today and the kinds of things we’ll see available in-game,” he says.

Cheung has budgeted a full eight hours to play the game as soon as it debuts at midnight. “I’ll probably spend much longer choosing the clothes than I need to,” he claims.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that food writer Rachel Gurjar made this goat kari for her “lifelong idol” Madhur Jaffrey, the renowned Indian cookbook author, at a dinner Gurjar hosted in her Brooklyn apartment in September 2022. When Jaffrey asked for the recipe, Gurjar knew she had to include it in her debut cookbook, East to East.

You can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

Recent findings suggest that while you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.

#19696. How Astronaut Reid Wiseman Keeps His Cool in Outer Space

How Astronaut Reid Wiseman Keeps His Cool in Outer Space

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4108 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.
  • During the three years that Reid Wiseman prepped for April’s Artemis II mission—for which he led a crew of three other astronauts nearly 700,000 miles, around the far side of the moon—he memorized everything from lunar geography to the Orion capsule’s elaborate controls.
  • “If I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral-buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, my world starts to shrink down,” says Wiseman.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.

During the three years that Reid Wiseman prepped for April’s Artemis II mission—for which he led a crew of three other astronauts nearly 700,000 miles, around the far side of the moon—he memorized everything from lunar geography to the Orion capsule’s elaborate controls. But, understandably, part of his training focused on not dying. Much of the mission “had no playbook at all,” says the recently retired astronaut. Still, he did have a few mantras to guide him. Here are two.

The first: Do uncomfortable things. “If I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral-buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, my world starts to shrink down,” says Wiseman. Meaning he gets better at managing stress by…seeking out stress. “The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things,” he explains. “You can even find it in a difficult conversation with a coworker—anything that gets that anxiety going.”.

In a recent development, but embracing challenges doesn’t always guarantee success. After Wiseman and his team failed to survive a couple of flight simulators, they adopted an old aviation saying: No fast hands. “If you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick,” Wiseman indicates. But to counter any rash decisions, you should first “just watch the second hand on the clock moving around.” The point is to pause before making a high-stakes judgment call. “If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds,” he says. “Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed.”.

Wiseman put the mantra to use during the mission when the Orion sprang a propellant leak. “Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away,” he states. He recalls how a crewmember began executing an emergency response, only for Wiseman to hit pause. Surveying the instruments, they realized the leak was minor and not worthy of a red alert reaction. “That was a good example of ‘Let’s be patient here for a minute.’ ” Take a beat and you’re more likely to think clearly—and come out alive.

Sources indicate that we chatted with Wiseman—who will begin a new deputy role at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Nov. 30—about his method for memorizing the Orion’s intricate control panels, the Artemis II crew’s pre-launch heart-to-hearts, and how writing poetry about the moon helped him do his job that much better.

Sources indicate that reid Wiseman: Actually, I mean, we’re still subject to the laws of gravity. We’re not feeling the effects of gravity.

It has been revealed that first and foremost is just, I don’t want to use the CrossFit model of “Be comfortable being uncomfortable,” but you do have to do things that are uncomfortable, and you have to continually do that. I have noticed if I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, that my world starts to shrink down. This is probably a side tangent, but my younger daughter suffered from anxiety pretty bad, and I remember the therapist saying: “You got to keep her moving. She’s got to get outside, she’s got to ride a bike, she’s got to go on a walk.” And I was watching her world shrink down, and I think it’s a corollary to what we do as astronauts. We’re flying planes, a lot of us are skydivers—I am not—and you just stay uncomfortable, stay in confined environments, and then stay really engaged in team skills, keep your mind going. The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things.

Yeah, for instance, I was just over in Switzerland. I do not like heights, I really do not like heights. And my girlfriend was pushing me to go on this rock climbing thing up the side of the Alps called Via Ferrata. You’re clipped into metal. You’re safe, but if you fall, you’re going to hurt yourself at least a little bit. And the whole time I was thinking: I do not want to do this, I have to do this. I went and did it. It was exhilarating, absolutely exhilarating. I was proud of myself at the end of it.

I do still look for those challenges. I definitely look for, if I haven’t done something before, that is usually motivation to try it, to lean into those sorts of things. You can even find it in just a difficult conversation with a coworker or with another human, anything that gets that anxiety going, gets the adrenaline up, something that you don’t want to do, but then you confront it and do it, there is a reward trigger at the end of that that is powerful.

I’m a huge conflict avoider, so it’s a struggle for me to meet those head on.

According to recent reports, into courage of confronting people. I don’t know. People in my office, there’s some people that thrive on it, and they do it great, doesn’t even bother them. And then, I don’t like confronting people, I figure everybody’s trying their best and if they’re getting on my nerves, it’s probably something wrong with me.

About five years ago, I just started reading books around the topics that I’m dealing with at work, and now that is my thing. I’m probably a book a week, usually audiobook, as I’m driving to and from work, but it’s on the stuff like small-team dynamics, it’s on learning environments, a lot of Carol Dweck stuff, on learning organizations, learning environments, and it’s been shocking to me how much that ties into confidence at work.

Somebody, somewhere will say, “Hey, you should read a book about this.” I’ll take a recommendation from a friend. [NASA’s] Anne McClain is a fellow astronaut, and she’s really cerebral, so she’s had a few good ones. [Retired Canadian Astronaut Corps astronaut] Jeremy Hansen, who I flew in space with, [NASA astronaut] Victor Glover’s had a few good ones. [NASA astronaut] Christina Koch has given me a few. So we all kind of trade book recommendations. And then as a crew, there were a few books that we all read as a crew, and it gave us a common language, a way to talk about things together, which was pretty powerful.

Christina had us read [retired NASA astronaut] Eileen Collins’s book, which is a very basic simple book, but it’s Through the Glass Ceiling Into the Stars, about her journey and some of the struggles that she had, and it really gave us a common language there. Then I recommended Growth Mindset by Carol Dweck. I quoted that book so many times, I think my crew all pretty much read it.

It was more in training. When we got onto the mission, we were glued together. We worked with operational psychologists before the mission, we’ve talked about a lot of this stuff and how powerful it was. We worked with a poet, we’ve worked with spiritual researchers, and cultural researchers about the moon. All that stuff just built a shared knowledge, shared understanding. But back to your original question, what do I do? I really do like to read books, I really do get a lot out of them, or at least listen to books.

In a recent development, it’s almost like meditation, but it’s not. But it would really soothe me. And I think in some ways, probably listening to a book or reading a book, it is an ultimate distraction from the thousands of things going on in my mind at all times. I think most astronauts are probably ADHD to some degree, but it’s a way to just put all that stuff aside and let my brain relax in a different direction for a little while.

Industry observers note that we had a lot of parts that had no playbook at all on this mission. I think the first answer to your question is, you have to work at it, and memorization tools. For lunar geography features, I made note cards. I have to make the study tools. If somebody hands me study tools, it doesn’t work. I need that function from eyes to brain, to hand, back to eyes to brain. That’s very vital for me.

For controls and displays for the Orion spacecraft, I would sit there on Saturdays, on my couch, with a blank sheet of paper, and in my head I would envision every display, and I would start writing every note of every column of every element of data on the display, and then I would check the manual and say, “All right, I’m wrong here, or I missed this….” And over time, that is just setting in stone in my brain where that is.

According to recent reports, for emergency procedures, we developed a lot of different techniques as a crew, but two things that are germane to this. First, Victor Glover came up with the mantra of, What is the first right step? So, you’ve got a fire on the spacecraft, there’s a lot of things that matter right now, but what’s the first right step that we all need to act on right now to start combating this fire? It is pretty cool in your brain, if you just really solidify the first right step, all the other steps will come. I was just at a Brandi Carlile concert, and she was saying when she sits down at the piano, if she thinks about what she’s about to play, she can’t do it. But if she sits down and just watches her hands, they will start playing the song. I find that with emergency procedures, if you know the first step to take, usually you can follow on with the rest of the right steps.

According to recent reports, then we also had a really strong mantra that was forged in a couple simulators that did not go well, where we did not survive the simulator, and that is: No fast hands. That’s an aviation motto, where if you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick, and they train you, the first thing you should do is just watch the secondhand on the clock moving around, or just go slow.

In a recent development, and so, we had a suspense, what is the criticality of our next action? If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds. Some actions require a split second, they require less than a second. So, those are the ones that we really need to hone in the simulator. But even in space, we had a few malfunctions, and we very deliberately executed, no fast hands. Let’s think about what the spacecraft is telling us. Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed. And only when we absolutely must make a decision, let’s make that decision.

The fire alarm, that was a great example of the first right step. When the fire alarm went off, we heard the emergency tone, and immediately Victor and I went to the displays. That is what we were trained to do. And I remarked, “We have a fire alarm,” and immediately Jeremy and Christina started looking for smoke, or smelling around the far side of the spacecraft to see if they could determine any location for fire, because we didn’t see any. We didn’t smell any. And that was incredible to watch us all act on the first right step principle.

On the no fast hands, it was the middle of the night, and a warning came up. It’s called a runbox failure. That doesn’t matter, but it basically means propellant is being used, but it’s being used outside the parameters of where it should be. So we have a leak somewhere. Either in propellant or pressurization.

Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away. Jeremy started executing the memorized response because it’s a very critical thing. I remarked, “Let’s just stop for a second. Let’s see what the vehicle is telling us.”.

Sources indicate that and Jeremy stopped, and we looked at all of our instrumentation. Pressures were stable, fuel was stable. So, if we did have a leak, it was a very small leak. Turns out we did have a leak, and it was a very small leak. That was a good example of “Let’s be patient here for a minute.” We know what we need to do, but let’s hang on and not do it quite yet.

Those times of lost communication do not bother us. We do train for those, those don’t bother us. I do want to talk for just a second about risk. Look, that mission was risky. We were pretty sure we were going to make it, but it was risky. So, before that, before we launched, we did talk as a crew very openly. We talked to our families very openly about risk—what happens if I don’t come back. I’ve been very public about that. I had a will, I told my kids what the life insurance plans were, where are you going to go if I don’t come back? Who’s going to take care of you? To me, those are conversations that are very powerful. And I think if you get to the launchpad with all of that stuff organized in your brain, you’re very at peace. And all four of us a few days before launch, we all shared the common feeling of peace.

Sources indicate that it was very weird. It was not nerves, tension, anxiety. It was peace. Two days before we launched, Jeremy Hansen, at dinner, asked all of us, the crew together, “Hey, let’s talk for a second about how are we going to handle it if we know we’re going to die, but we’ve got a couple days before it’s going to happen.” Almost Apollo 13. We have a failure. We know we’re not going to survive, and we have several days. And it was a pretty quick conversation. We were like, “Let’s just do it with dignity and give each other as much grace as we can because we don’t know how we’re going to react, but dignity. Let’s come back to just doing it with dignity.” Who ever has a conversation like that?

And the four of us had that conversation, and very rapidly, we all aligned behind dignity, that is how we’re going to approach this, but we’re also going to have grace because we’re not in that situation right now. We do not know how people are going to handle it. I mean, I could have a total terror attack, a panic attack, you don’t know. But the fact that we were in a place where we could talk about that stuff was very powerful, probably because we’re all around 50, we felt very accomplished in our lives, and very satisfied with where we were. We introduced overwhelmingly at peace.

Not quite that aggressive, but exhausting, yes.

It’s a number of things. First, the four of us were all very committed to excellence and to being there for each other. Even if we didn’t always show it, we always committed to it. We talked a lot about wanting to launch as friends and land as friends. That’s a bit of lip service, but it was a motto that we tried to uphold. We’re just never going to give up on each other. We’re going to work on this for the rest of our lives. And then, in training, we often joke that we were like the basketball Olympic dream team, where you took all the best players from basketball, put them together, and they were a terrible team.

Recent findings suggest that for quite a while, we were just not a great team, but we were working on it. I bore a lot of responsibility of that as a commander. Like, why can’t I get these people in line? But also with this crew of experienced and senior astronauts, I couldn’t just say, “You’re getting in line.” It just wasn’t going to work. And I didn’t want that, I wanted us all to be ourselves. Each one of us brings an individual richness into this tapestry of this crew, and I wanted that to show through.

I was willing to deal with some pain and agony over crew dynamics if it meant everyone showing up at the end together. I think that did pay off very well. So, we noticed pretty early on that we had these crew dynamics issues, and we set up a couple extra meetings with our...at NASA, we have these people called BHP, behavioral health and performance folks. They’re all psychologists, operational psychologists.

We set up some meetings with them. They had all these guided points. The first question they asked us, I don’t think they ever asked us another question, we tore ourselves apart. I think every member of the crew cried at some point. We exhausted ourselves, and they were like, Wow, you guys really have some concerns we need to work through. So, we did more meetings with them, and we did work through a lot of that stuff. We didn’t work through all of it. But what that process revealed with those behavioral health folks is our willingness, our commitment to each other. I didn’t need us to launch perfect, I just needed us to be committed to each other.

It has been revealed that then, I will throw in this one thing a few months before launch, because I also think this was important: We spent a lot of time giving each other feedback. But before launch, I wanted to make sure we also shifted to meeting each other where we are. I mean, you can tell me how to change for the next 10 years. At some point though, I have a personality that is just who I am. I’m going to work every day to be better, but at some point, I think you need to meet me where I am, and I need to meet you where you are. And we did that, and that was very powerful as well. By the time we came off the launchpad in that vehicle, we were really, really, really together. We didn’t have to be. I know there’s been a lot of crews that haven’t been, but we were.

That’s very well stated. Because our crew conversations were harder than any technical matter that we had to solve in this training at least.

According to recent reports, yes, but I won’t read it, although some of them were actually very good. We talked to a professor of English, Chris Cokinos, at the University of Arizona. But he held quite a few workshops with us, and he gave us drills. I wrote him an email a couple days ago just thanking him for allowing us to express creativity in the ways that we saw the world and the moon. And his stuff was all focused on the moon. How do you relay the moon in the five senses? And how do you do it in a way that captures imagination?

Industry observers note that in the end, we’re all kind of philosophers, and it just helped us be a little bit more creative in the way we saw things, and it reinforced to us that you can find beauty if you’re looking for it. I love the way Chris Cokinos framed for us the beauty of the moon. Because an engineer or a geologist could have framed it as a barren, stark, celestial body, but Chris framed it as a magnificent, beautiful, celestial neighbor. And just having that sense and that feeling really showed through when we were out there.

I kept a journal on my computer on the mission, just putting, remember, every day, just think about sight, smell, touch, taste, feel, and go through those every day in this vehicle. Sadly, the computers were so hard to use in space, I did not journal on that even a singular time. But basically every day we would do a five senses kind of thing, and you could be in the middle of a simulator, and I would pull out my notebook and just jot. All right, I just did this docking maneuver. And that docking maneuver, that’s the most technical thing you can do. What was the sight, smell, sound? And wow, all of a sudden you start pulling out tons of data that you otherwise would’ve neglected.

According to recent reports, it is starting to abate a little bit. But we were doing an outdoor podcast, getting interviewed in this beautiful setting in California, and a little breeze came from left to right across my face, and I was like, “Man, that feels incredible.” And I never would’ve noticed that even. I was walking around Latest York City, and I saw some tulips coming up out of the ground, and I was stopped dead in my tracks for a few seconds just looking at them, thinking about how impossible it is that, in this brown dirt, these beautiful green sprouts are coming up, and it’s like the birth of spring, and summer’s here. It was like, why am I focusing on all this? But I was focusing on all of that.

Industry observers note that I say this all the time when we’re out talking to the general public, but in Apollo, those guys talked about peace and joy and hope, and then we went out there and we talked about peace and joy and hope. I just think if you’re a quarter million miles away looking back at this impossibly unique planet, it’s the only words that we have in the English language that can convey even a small portion of what that felt like.

Industry observers note that we saw sights on the far side of the moon, and especially when the sun eclipsed behind the moon that I can’t even describe the beauty, especially of that eclipse. It was otherworldly. And when I look at the moon now, I still think about that. I know when the right side of the moon is lit up at night, but not the left side of the moon, I almost don’t even look at it because we didn’t see that. But when the left side of the moon is lit up, that is very relatable to me, and I know what’s on that other side now.

Sources indicate that we only saw 18% of the far side on the left side, but I know what that looks like back there, and I think about it all the time. The moon became more of a friend when we were around it, I just felt comradeship with the moon. It was revealing its secrets to us. We were seeing parts of it that it doesn’t reveal to people on Earth, but we were seeing them, and it was very powerful.

Yeah. I think about all my family, all my friends, and now that I’ve talked to you on this, I’ll think about you next time I look at the moon.

It’s the old TV. It’s the thing that we can look at from anywhere on Earth and we know we’re all seeing the exact same picture. I used to look at that and think about my brother when he went away to college, and I’ve always loved that. I was in the Navy; I love being at sea and watching the moon rise over the ocean when it’s just reflecting off the ocean. The moon’s a very powerful, very beautiful thing to get to look at. To me, it’s more a peace and togetherness than anything. ✦.

Surviving space is a group effort, and Wiseman has often sought expert wisdom on problems “he’s dealing with at work.” Before retiring in September, he averaged a book a week, which he usually listened to while commuting to and from the Johnson Space Center in Houston. If a book really hit, the rest of his crew might read it too—effectively forming the world’s most high-functioning book club.

#19695. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

📅 13 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (383 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Epicurious ↗ Open Full Page

Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (383 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights.
  • Recent findings suggest that the seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home.
  • More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

Recent findings suggest that the seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

According to recent reports, ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#19694. Holiday Campaigns: Can Luxury’s Hand-Drawn Holiday Campaigns Really Rebuff AI?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2172 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

Holiday Campaigns: Can Luxury’s Hand-Drawn Holiday Campaigns Really Rebuff AI?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • That’s the message brands are sending this holiday season, as luxury turns to hand-drawn illustrations and stop-motion animation for its batch of festive holiday campaigns.
  • As audiences filled theaters to watch animation studio Laika’s Wildwood, which ended with close-up clips of (literal) human hands crafting the puppets featured in the film, a host of luxury brands released holiday campaigns in step with this emphasis on human craftsmanship.
  • It has been revealed that prada got in first before Halloween with a holiday campaign for which the brand commissioned a group of artists led by cinematic animator John Pomeroy (known for his work at Walt Disney Animation Studios and Sullivan Bluth Studios, which he co-founded).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Have a happy, handmade holiday!

That’s the message brands are sending this holiday season, as luxury turns to hand-drawn illustrations and stop-motion animation for its batch of festive holiday campaigns.

As audiences filled theaters to watch animation studio Laika’s Wildwood, which ended with close-up clips of (literal) human hands crafting the puppets featured in the film, a host of luxury brands released holiday campaigns in step with this emphasis on human craftsmanship.

It has been revealed that prada got in first before Halloween with a holiday campaign for which the brand commissioned a group of artists led by cinematic animator John Pomeroy (known for his work at Walt Disney Animation Studios and Sullivan Bluth Studios, which he co-founded). Dior followed suit with a holiday film directed by Oscar-nominated animator Sylvain Chomet. Loewe released a collection in partnership with Tim Burton, an interpretation of his seminal The Nightmare Before Christmas, with a documentary about Burton’s work accompanying. Rimowa created miniature worlds inside its suitcases, all done by hand.

All of the campaigns placed emphasis on human touch — as did the communication surrounding them. “A Prada fantasy, created by hand,” Prada’s release read, citing inspiration “from the human core of storytelling at the heart of the holiday season”, celebrating hand-drawn illustration for its anachronism and romanticism. Loewe emphasized the film’s handmade puppets and handcrafted sets, and likened this to the brand’s own relationship to craft. It’s trickled down the fashion funnel, with brands from Pamela Anderson’s skincare brand Sonsie to Barbour tapping this technique.

Prada tapped animator John Pomeroy to lead its “Drawing Prada: Animated by Hand” campaign.

According to recent reports, this was Rimowa’s fifth year collaborating with artists for its holiday campaign, most of which have been 2D animations. This year, the brand wanted to level up, introducing handcrafted miniature worlds from clay, paper, felt and wood. “From a technical point of view, it was quite challenging to go from a 2D animation to creating a full 3D world with puppets,” notes CMO Mathieu Plenier: over 30 artists, about 200 hours of work that went into its creation, plus a week filming across two film stages to make the films. Many of this year’s campaigns cite similarly lengthy production processes.

For Prada, this process was part of the draw. “The idea was to celebrate and display a creative process that would in itself create a sense of wonder,” a Prada spokesperson tells Vogue Business, noting that hand-drawn animation felt like the best way to do so because of its sense of touch and association with craft. Pomeroy was a no-brainer because of his deep understanding of “old school” 2D animation, they add. “John has described animation as a collaborative art form that takes many hands and many hours to complete, and it is because of that collaboration that animation is a marvelous endeavor.”.

“It’s a universally beloved, nostalgic approach to signaling ‘we’re human, we believe in human creativity’ and to position the brand as anti-AI,” says Michael Scanlon, chief creative officer at creative studio Chandelier Creative, of the influx of illustrated and animated campaigns this season.

According to recent reports, to Ariella Starkman, founder and creative director of creative production tech giant Starkman & Associates, it’s less a response to AI itself than the anxiety the tech induces. “They are a response to a larger cultural anxiety about what AI represents: the coldness, the automation, the one-size-fits-all approach, mixed with a very real fear of losing our jobs and feeling replaceable,” she claims. “Deeply spooky.”.

Rimowa’s holiday films were made in collaboration with animation studio Studio Linguini.

The campaign showcases the journeys toward whatever destination its characters are heading.

It has been revealed that these fears aren’t without basis. This year, brands have leaned into ‘effort signaling’ with their marketing, from edible art to hand-drawn illustrations, to indicate to their consumers that they are putting time and care into their creative. While appealing to shoppers’ emotions, effort signaling fails to alleviate these very real concerns Starkman highlights, about the state of the world they’re living and shopping in. One anonymous creative director, who runs the account Dank Art Director Memes, leveled a similar critique at this year’s crafty holiday campaigns, flagging the disjuncture between campaigns designed to “humanwash” their image after a year of layoffs and high-speed AI adoption.

Industry observers note that as a marketing mechanism, these crafty campaigns are effective — when done right. But the state of the world into which luxury brands are releasing this content places an onus on these businesses to foster and embrace creativity behind the scenes as they do in their communications.

In a recent development, brands positioning themselves as meticulous about craft by commissioning artists is nothing newly introduced, notes Quentin Jones, illustrator and founder of House of Quentin Jones. “People have been drawn to tactile, handmade imagery online for a long time. When I graduated in 2012, brands were already commissioning me to make beauty campaigns for digital platforms rather than working with traditional photographers, because they knew people would stop and look at something where they could feel the human touch,” she says. But, she observes, the prevalence of overly polished AI work has heightened the instinct toward the artist’s hand.

Industry observers note that “It’s a reaction to the sameness of digital worlds,” Scanlon agrees. “Hand-drawn and stop motion animation have a certain kind of imperfection that makes you feel. It triggers an emotion, and I think a lot of brands are struggling to emotionally connect right now.”.

In a recent development, for Starkman, this offering of nostalgia — “like cartoons on a Sunday morning when you have no school the next day” — is telling. “The holiday season is one of the most commercially significant periods of the year for many brands, so it’s very interesting — and telling — that they’re leading with feeling rather than product,” she says. “Brands are realizing that making people feel something is just as important as getting them to buy something.” Starkman recently wrapped a campaign for a major luxury brand where one of the main requests was to create something that made you feel something, she says.

Tim Burton illustrating his original Nightmare Before Christmas characters.

Loewe licensed Tim Burton’s original illustrations for the collection.

According to recent reports, “There’s something very special about animation, particularly at Christmas. It connects us to childhood and a shared imagination,” states Elisa Valenzuela, illustrator and founder of motion studio Studio Convergences. “It allows even the most serious and demanding luxury houses to embrace fantasy, humor and a certain lightness.”.

This was at the core of Rimowa’s campaign, Plenier indicates. “With this campaign, we wanted to connect the holiday with human emotions, thinking about a more enjoyable, struggle-free life. Blending the tangible with the imaginative, the campaign invites viewers to celebrate life’s simple daily pleasures.” The idea then is that gifting a Rimowa suitcase will “feel like gifting an invitation to travel and explore upcoming worlds”, he adds.

It has been revealed that for its holiday campaign, Scottish handbag brand Strathberry tapped stop-motion artist Alina Golovlova for the fifth time; and her second holiday campaign. “Making by hand is at the core of our brand, so partnering with artists and craftspeople is hugely important to us in any creative project,” notes co-founder Leeanne Hundleby, who was especially drawn to felt stop motion for how highly specialized it is. “We wanted to champion the patience and skill it takes to make something truly by hand.”.

A still from Strathberry’s three-part series with stop motion artist Alina Golovlova.

It has been revealed that over the past year, Valenzuela has noted growing enthusiasm for animation, craft, stop motion and images that, she states, embrace imperfection. “What’s slightly paradoxical is that so many brands seem to be embracing these techniques at the same time,” she says. “A desire for individuality is becoming a collective trend.” It’s not necessarily a bad thing, she says, noting that this is often how creative movements evolve.

Still, Scanlon hopes to see brands venture into an array of hand-crafted techniques, not solely animation. “Anti-AI approaches don’t need to be so obvious. Animation is an incredible, timeless craft, but it also feels like an easy route for a brand. You can see the strategy on the sleeve,” he states. “The world needs more and other kinds of practical magic. Stagecraft, surrealism, handmade spectacle.”.

For all the brand comms about the time and effort that go into these campaigns, they’re not without scrutiny at a moment when audiences are hyper-aware of the potential for AI augmentation.

According to recent reports, dior’s film, for one, was not met with the reception the brand might have hoped for. Audiences fast pointed out flaws in the film they believed to stem from AI use: a sixth finger on a character’s hand; glitches between frames. Commentators were quick to hop on their soapboxes to drag Dior for promoting the film as hand-drawn. Chomet told Variety that the film did not use generative AI, but used automated interpolation in a “very small part” of the process. Dior did not respond to requests for comment.

Recent findings suggest that for all of the online warriors’ grievances, some illustrators are unconvinced by the uproar. “I find this debate interesting, but also rather sad, because it risks overshadowing the work and talent of the artist involved,” Valenzuela says. Traditional animation involves production time that can’t be compressed, she says, noting that the time it takes to draw, build sets or animate objects frame by frame doesn’t always align with commercial production schedules. “I think it’s a shame if the occasional use of AI is enough to call an entire artistic project into question.”.

Jones doesn’t believe it’s a matter of handmade versus AI. “I see nothing wrong with an image-maker using AI as one of their tools, much as we use Photoshop, After Effects or Premiere. It’s another way of getting an idea out of your head and into the world,” she claims. The key is not to use the tech in the creation of the artwork itself. “So much of the magic happens in the process of making.”.

For Prada, though the starting point was “the human core of storytelling”, the brand is under no illusions about the context into which the campaign was released. “We can understand why people are looking closely at this concept with AI in mind, particularly given the wider conversation around AI and creative work at the moment. What is interesting for us is the degree of attention people are paying to craft and the creative process, and we think that’s a positive conversation to be having,” the spokesperson notes, adding that Prada didn’t use the tech in the campaign’s creation. “We are very comfortable being transparent about that process.”.

According to recent reports, anyone working with handmade elements today does also need to be digitally fluent — especially when the work is ultimately going to be consumed digitally, Jones argues. “It’s about having the taste and skill to use everything at your disposal without letting the technology dictate the aesthetic,” she states. “What people are craving isn’t necessarily the absence of technology, but the presence of a human being. We need to preserve both the human touch and the human intention behind the work.”.

Looking ahead, Starkman is acutely aware of how “terrifyingly good” AI will get at replicating craft, human imperfection, and all the visual cues we at the moment associate with ‘authentic’ creative expression, she says. “What happens when we can no longer tell the difference? If something looks handmade and makes us feel something, does it matter whether a human actually made it?” she asks. “I think it does, but I also think we’re going to have to get much better at explaining why.”.

In a recent development, perhaps the why comes down to what’s going on behind the scenes, beyond the holidays: not just the painstaking hours of crafting a stop-motion animation, but at the brands commissioning these artistic works in the first place. “It all has to come from a truth in their product, their organization, and how the brand approaches creativity,” Scanlon states.

Sources indicate that take Hermès, which was Valenzuela’s first-ever animation client back in 2018 — back when AI was, to the average person, more of a lofty sci-fi trope than a sweeping threat to one’s livelihood. “They gave me my start in this field, and I think they’ve demonstrated for years how collaborating with artists and their distinctive creative worlds can beautifully express a house’s values,” she says. “It’s essential today to preserve our ability to dream, experiment, make mistakes and surprise ourselves. Whether we’re fashion designers or image-makers, perhaps our role is simply to keep bringing poetry and humanity into the world.”.
